55_interl150: the time of purification having first been completed, and the offering made in Jerusalem, which is passed over here
55_interl151: here Joseph is taken on not as husband but as foster-father and guardian
55_marg220: Wonderful humility of Christ. He flees who is the refuge of others; and virtue, by fleeing, teaches its own. Whence: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another.”
55_interl153: behold, that deceits are not hidden from God
55_marg221: Joseph is a figure of the preachers who carried Christ with his mother, that is, the faith of Christ and of the Church, to the Gentiles, leaving behind Herod, that is, the unbelief of the Jews.
55_marg222: Because he went down secretly by flight to illumine Egypt, leaving the night to the Jews.
55_marg223: He carried him by night into Egypt, because he left the night of ignorance to the unbelievers, from whom he himself withdrew. When he returns, no mention of night is made, because at the end of the world the Jews, receiving the faith as Christ returns from Egypt, will be enlightened. Here an example is given to the faithful of avoiding the fury of persecutors where it is expedient, as he himself says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another.” This flight of the Lord signifies that the elect are often to be driven from their seats by the wickedness of evil men. He flees as a man, whom a star had shown to be God a little before.
55_interl154: because the faith of Christ remained among the Gentiles, “until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in”
55_marg224: Showing God to be worshipped by every people, because Christ, not received by the Jews, passes to the Gentiles through preaching.
55_marg225: He flees into Egypt as he was born, so that he might repair corrupted nature. Thus he flees, so that he might recall the fugitives. That he fled was of the sacrament, not of fear, so that he might give his own an example of fleeing. He who came to die did not flee death; nor did he dread the snares, he who came to lay open the devil’s wiles. Of this flight Isaias foretold: “Behold the Lord will ascend upon a swift cloud,” that is, flesh without sin: “and will enter into Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be moved.” He lay hidden in Egypt for seven years.
55_interl155: until the end of unbelief, since Judea raged against the Church
55_interl156: consubstantial, since: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us”
55_marg226: “Out of Egypt have I called my son,” etc. In Osee this is found according to the Hebrew truth, or, as some assert, in the book of Numbers, since the whole was done by the arrangement of God.
55_marg227: It is likely that, since nothing had been reported to Herod by the magi, he believed they had been deceived by a deceitful star, and so had not returned to him. Whence he was quiet for so long from the search for the boy. Then, when the things said and done in the temple had been made public, he felt that he had been deceived by the magi; and hastening to Christ’s death, he killed the boys.
55_marg228: It is likely that a year and four days after the nativity of Christ, Herod raged against the boys; he perhaps postponed this because he had set out for Rome, or was accused there, or to consult the Romans about the things that were said of Christ.
55_marg229: Perhaps for this reason he kept himself so long from the search for the boy, so that he might seize him more anxiously, and he could in no way slip away.
55_interl157: from this his anger is heaped up, already troubled by the birth
55_interl158: he used his word for a sword
55_interl159: so that he who was born might not escape
55_marg230: As soon as Christ appeared to the world, persecution began against him, which prefigured the persecution of the saints; and while the infant is sought, the infants are slain, in whom the form of martyrdom is born, where the infancy of the Church is dedicated.
55_marg231: The death of the little ones figures the passion of all martyrs, who were slain as little ones, that is, humble and innocent, who suffered at the hands of the impious, whom Herod signifies, not only in Judea but everywhere. That they were two years old, because they were perfected in teaching and in works. With them slain, Christ escaped, because bodies can be killed, but divinity cannot be touched.
55_interl160: so that in so great a multitude he could not lie hidden
55_marg232: He is not content with laying waste Bethlehem; he laid waste the adjacent places too, and showed no mercy for age, from the son of a single night up to the son of two years, so that he might kill all.
55_marg233: So that he who had long been seeking him in so great a multitude might not escape. It is likely that this killing was done a year and four days after the Lord’s nativity. The death of the little ones figures the passion of all martyrs, who were slain as little ones, that is, humble and innocent, who suffered not only in Judea but everywhere at the hands of the impious, whom they signified; who were two years old, because perfected in teaching and in works. With them slain, Christ escapes, because bodies can be killed, but divinity cannot be touched.
55_interl161: so that he might be hidden neither by place nor by time
55_marg234: “From two years old and under.” For he feared that the boy, to whom the stars were servants, might change his appearance to a little above or below his age.
55_marg235: For bimatus is the space of two years; in Greek ‘ymates’ is what in Latin is called ‘annus’, a year.
55_marg236: Therefore ‘from two years old,’ so that, as Herod had occupied the boundaries of the city in advance, so he might also anticipate another year. Therefore also ‘from two years old,’ because he feared that the boy to whom the stars were servants might conform himself to a little above or below his age.
55_interl162: from the rising of the star
55_marg237: It is called fulfilled, because before it was made it was half-full to those reading, since what sounded in the letter secretly promised something to come.
55_marg238: In the seventh homily he says that the star appeared for a year, as at the destruction of the Romans signs appeared in the sky, when the voice of angels was heard: “Let us pass from these seats.”
55_marg239: That is, a voice spread far and wide on high.
55_marg240: Allegorically: or the voice of the Church, groaning over the slaughter of its members, rose up even to the throne of the supreme Judge.
55_marg241: Because of the Levite’s wife, slain through fornication and divided into twelve parts according to the number of the tribes, all Israel destroyed the tribe of Benjamin except three hundred men; the weeping and howling of the survivors was heard as far as Rama, which is a place near Gabaa, twelve miles from Bethlehem. “Was heard”: he exaggerates hyperbolically, so that Rachel, though already dead, is said by the feeling of a grieving mother to be now weeping for her sons. Whence through this a history is woven about the Chaldeans, that the devastation to come would be similar to the earlier slaughter of the Jewish people by them. But more truly, with the Spirit revealing it through the evangelist, the prophecy is taken as referring to the slaughter of the boys. He therefore says that then was fulfilled what was said; because although the word of the prophecy looks to the imminent captivity, yet in it, as in a shadow, the future truth of the slaughter of the infants is announced.
55_interl165: the lament resounding far and wide reached even to God
55_marg242: Because she was buried near Bethlehem, and from the earthly lodging of her body she received the name of mother. Or because many of Benjamin and of Joseph were slain. Benjamin was born of Rachel, and Bethlehem does not fall to his lot but only to the tribe of Judah. But because the tribes of Judah and Benjamin are neighbours on the borders of Bethlehem, many also of the tribe of Benjamin were slain.
55_marg243: Note that it is better to say “Rachel” than to say that Bethlehem wept: through her the figure of the sacrament is introduced, because through her the image of the Church is commended in all things, which weeps not so much for those carried off by death as for those destroyed by torment.
55_marg244: Rachel, that is the Church, weeps for her tender lambs who were destroyed, and “would not be comforted, because they are not” in the present; but she sends all her hope and consolation on to eternal life. Or she weeps and does not receive consolation, according to a twofold understanding of some: either because she judged them dead forever, or because she would not here be consoled in the present over those whom she knew would live forever. This fits the Church more truly, which grieves not only for the destroyed, but wishes to keep even more those whom she had brought forth, or to beget those not yet born, for whom there is no consolation, since they are eternally dead.
55_marg245: Allegorically: Rightly, moreover, Rachel, who is called ‘a sheep seeing God,’ signifies the Church, whose whole intention is to keep watch so that she may contemplate God; and she is the hundredth sheep which the shepherd carried back on his shoulders.
55_marg246: Rachel, that is the Church weeping for her slain. And so it was not a small matter for the prophet to foreshadow so great a mystery, though obscurely, with greater care.
55_marg247: The Church weeps and will not be comforted here, because her children are not of this world. Or she weeps because, while she is bearing, she has sorrow; whence it is said: “You shall lament and weep,” etc.; but comfort is added: “your sorrow shall be turned into joy.”
55_interl167: in such a way that they might be called back into the world
55_marg248: Because, when the faithlessness of the Jews is lulled to sleep, with Elias and Enoch preaching, Judea will receive the word of God.
55_marg249: When the king is dead, his accomplices perish at once; so, with the persecution ceasing, the Church is invited to heavenly things.
55_interl170: because it was not yet publicly revealed to whom the angel was entrusting this office
55_interl173: because scribes and Pharisees will plot the death of Christ with Herod
55_marg250: He does not specify in which direction, so that the angel returns while Joseph is in doubt, and by his frequent address Joseph is made more certain.
55_marg251: Because he did not specify which part, Joseph understood Judea, which was the more worthy part of the kingdom.
55_marg252: Some relate that Herod had the nobler men of the Jews put to death at his own funeral, so as to compel the Jews to weep for his death.
55_marg253: Allegorically. Joseph bears the figure of the apostles, by whose ministry Christ is carried about. The apostles first came into the land of Israel, because they first preached to the Jews. But because of Herod, that is, while the hereditary unbelief remains, they fear, and being warned withdraw to preach grace to the Gentiles and carry Christ over to them.
55_marg254: The land of Israel being named, it seemed to Joseph that such a child ought to dwell nowhere but in Jerusalem, where the temple and the reading of the prophets were. Yet the angel wished Galilee to be understood, which the Jews also inhabited; this shows that it had been so predestined, because “he shall be called a Nazarene.”
55_interl175: Herod, Philip, Archelaus and Lysanias were brothers
55_interl176: from which he thought himself warned
55_marg255: If he feared Judea because of Archelaus, heir of his father’s cruelty, why not also Galilee, where another brother of his, Herod, reigned? Because Archelaus, after his father, obtained the monarchy of the whole kingdom; but growing insolent, he was deposed by Tiberius Caesar and sent into exile at Lugdunum; and then the kingdom was divided into four tetrarchies, of which one, that is Galilee, his brother Herod obtained.
55_marg256: It is asked: why did Joseph not fear to go into Galilee as into Judea, since Archelaus reigned there too? But he could better lie hidden in Nazareth, which was remote, than in Jerusalem, where the seat of the kingdom was and Archelaus was constantly present.
55_interl177: the angel does not change the command, but more plainly corrects the error of piety
55_interl178: which is also the land of Israel, because the people of Israel inhabited it too
55_marg257: That Christ is not carried there where Archelaus reigned signifies that Christ will be hidden from those in whom Antichrist will reign.
55_marg258: Nazareth is interpreted as ‘new shoot’ or ‘flower of the field’, from whose root it is read that the Holy of Holies sprang, to signify the substance of his eternity. Therefore, as he chose the time and the place of his birth, so also the city in which he grew up, whose name is a sign that he, holiness itself, nurtured in holiness, is rightly called ‘Holy of Holies.’ Whence also his disciples were first called ‘Nazarenes,’ but afterwards were called Christians from Christ.
55_marg259: Nazareth in Galilee, to which he is transferred, signifies the part of the same people that was about to receive the faith. Whence it is interpreted ‘flower’, because the Church, the more ardently she passes from earthly to heavenly things, the more she abounds in the flower and shoot of virtues.
55_marg260: He says ‘prophets’ in the plural, because we do not have a fixed example in Scripture; this shows that he took the sense, not the words. Or in the same words in Isaias according to the Hebrew truth: “There shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a Nazarene shall rise up out of his root.”
55_interl180: Nazarene, that is ‘holy’, which befits Christ
55_interl181: while he still dwelt in Nazareth
55_marg261: He passes over much, and goes on to the preaching of John.
55_marg262: He comprehends not only the years of childhood but all up to the preaching of John, that is, when he was almost thirty years old. Luke expresses the times more significantly: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar.”
55_interl182: see what he did on coming
55_marg263: He revealed himself, who had previously been silent, by baptizing and preaching, preparing the way for the Lord.
55_interl183: thus noting that the desert suits penitents
55_marg264: In the desert of Judea, because the Jews were forsaken by God, and for them penance is necessary that they may return.
55_interl184: let each punish the evils of his former life, because the salvation we lost will draw near, and the chance of returning whence we fell
55_marg265: The herald announces what the truth itself afterwards proclaimed.
55_marg266: Penance comes first; the promise of the kingdom follows. He who truly repents punishes his past errors in himself, and then raises his mind to the heavenly kingdom.
55_marg267: If remission is given freely in baptism, why is penance preached? But penance is threefold. The first: to renounce and condemn errors and all evils before baptism, which is necessary for those coming to Christ. The second: that after baptism those who have fallen be renewed through penance. The third, by which the saints are purged daily of such sins, without which life is not lived.
55_marg268: To repent is to lament deeds done before and not to commit what is to be lamented. The kingdom of heaven is said to be at hand for penitents, not earthly things as in the old law, and this through the obedience of Christ. And this kingdom of heaven John first preached.
55_marg269: The first virtue is, through penance, to destroy the old man and to hate vices; whoever does not do this does not only fail to grasp the virtues, but does not even escape punishments. The virtue of penance is conceived by fear, which is “the beginning of wisdom.” Penance is from punishing, by which each one punishes what he has committed unlawfully.
55_marg270: To do penance is to bring forth worthy fruits of penance. The kingdom of heaven, that is Christ, through whom the saints reign in the heavens; or the gospel, by which he invites to the kingdom.
55_interl186: by this promise souls are lifted up: “the kingdom of God is within you”
55_marg271: so he preached, for so the prophet foretold of him
55_marg272: Unless it had drawn near, no one could return, since the weak and the blind lacked the way, which is Christ; John, preparing that way, puts penance before it.
55_interl187: so he preached, for so the prophet foretold of him
55_interl188: the herald of the word; the word goes before
55_interl189: because the word went before, the herald of the word
55_marg273: John is the voice; Christ is the ‘Word’, who cries out in John.
55_marg274: No word is heard without a voice, nor does a voice avail without understanding of the word.
55_marg275: The voice prepares the way for the word, that it may be received. Whence: “I have prepared a lantern for my Christ.”
55_interl190: because the desert of Judea announces the consolation of redemption
55_interl191: because it announces the consolation of redemption to Judea, now deserted
55_marg276: A pattern for penitents: the place of their way of life is not a crowd of men, but the desert. Clothing not soft for luxury, but rough; food scant and unusual.
55_marg277: Typically. The desert signifies the life of the saints, set apart from the allurements of the world.
55_interl192: cast off crooked things; do upright works
55_interl195: faith is the way by which the Word ascends to the heart
55_marg278: Prepare the way. Cast off wickednesses; receive faith and good works; make straight, so that you do not serve earthly things.
55_marg279: The way of the Lord is directed to the heart when his word is diligently heard.
55_interl196: that is, change your manners for the better, and so the paths will be made straight
55_marg280: And the same John, etc. He who preaches penance displays the habit of penance. In him the cheapness of clothing and food is praised, the use of which is condemned in the rich.
55_marg281: John instructs penitents in himself and sets forth a pattern of life, dwelling in the desert, living on locusts, clothed in camel’s hair.
55_marg282: A servant of God ought not to have clothing for adornment or for delight, but only to cover nakedness. Hence John was clothed in hair.
55_marg283: Morally. In John’s garment we are admonished to use rough things to restrain the flesh; in food, that we use not artfully prepared but natural foods.
55_marg284: Morally. Dress and food show a way of life. He is clothed in rough things, because he did not coax vices but reproved them with harsh rebuke, thus: “Ye brood of vipers,” etc. A girdle of skin about the loins, because he crucified his flesh with vices and lusts. He eats honey and locusts, because his preaching tasted sweet to the crowds while he was thought to be Christ. But he soon fell, because he appeared not to be Christ but his herald. In honey is sweetness; in the locust a lively flight, but soon falling.
55_marg285: not of wool, because this is a sign of austerity, that of softer luxury
55_interl201: a girdle of skin is made from the dead skin of an animal, scraped of flesh and blood
55_interl202: the loins are the pleasure of sin, because sin is committed in pleasure
55_interl204: not prepared with care, but as befits a hermit
55_marg287: from tree trunks or from herbs
55_marg288: Then went out, because unless one goes out from evils, one is not washed. Whence fittingly follows: they were baptized by him in the Jordan, which is interpreted as descent, because they descended from the pride of the old man to the humility of confession and amendment. For already then an example was given to those to be baptized, of confessing sins and promising better things.
55_interl205: on account of the novelty of the preaching and the roughness of his clothing and food
55_interl206: the baptism going before, not forgiving sins
55_marg289: In the Jordan, because in it the figure of baptism went before, and from its name it demands a descent from pride, which suits those baptized.
55_marg290: The confession of sins is the testimony of a conscience that fears God. For whoever fears God’s judgment is not ashamed to confess sins. Perfect fear dissolves all shame. Confession of sin carries shame, and that very blushing is a heavy punishment. Therefore we are commanded to confess sins, so that we suffer blushing as a punishment; for this very thing is part of divine judgment.
55_marg291: These are among the heretics of the Jews, because the Pharisees prefer the justice of observances and traditions. Whence the Pharisees are also called, that is, separated from the people by a private justice. Sadducees, that is, just ones; for they claim for themselves what they are not. These deny the resurrection, saying the soul perishes with the body; they accept the five books of Moses and reject the prophets. John rebukes these when they come to baptism, because they most of all needed correction and penance.
55_marg292: “Ye brood of vipers,” etc. That is, poisoned sons of the poisoned, because they envy the good and persecute them, and harm their neighbours as their fathers did.
55_marg293: The viper kills its father; so did the Jews to the prophets, who were their fathers.
55_interl208: no one, because you do not repent; but without penance you will not escape wrath
55_interl209: as if none but the Son of God, whom I announce to you
55_interl211: so that thus you may escape
55_marg294: Bede. As if to say: why do you not first lay down your poisons, so that you may come to baptism? “Bring forth fruit,” not of any kind but worthy. For the fruit of good work ought not to be equal in one who has sinned nothing or less, and in one who has fallen more grievously. But the Jews, glorying in Abraham, are unwilling to acknowledge themselves sinners. Whence he adds: “And think not to say,” etc. He provokes them to humility; for in pride there is no penance.
55_marg295: There is discernment in penance, which sets before the eyes the fear of God and the dread of punishments, recalling the shame of old. So the sorrow of the heart breaks out into weeping, because there are no wounds without pain, unless the vital parts of the limbs are dead around them; it is grace that feels, and feeling, it seeks health.
55_interl213: according to the measure of the fault; this comes from the discretion that is necessary for the penitent
55_interl215: and do not trust in the seed of Abraham, as if salvation came from this alone
55_marg296: For I tell you. He draws them away from the flesh, so that they may consider the works of God’s predestination. The first are the rudiments of faith: to believe that God can do whatever he wills, so that he who created all things out of nothing can form sons of Abraham from stones or from dust.
55_interl216: because these are not the sons of the flesh in the seed, but those who are sons of God. Whence he adds: “God is able,” etc.
55_interl217: to the Gentiles, whose hearts were insensible
55_marg297: Demonstrative: to those stones which Josue caused to be carried from the Jordan, to which, as if extending a finger, he speaks.
55_marg298: Josue caused twelve stones to be carried from the midst of the Jordan to the land, and others from the land to be put back in the same bed; through these is foreshadowed the blindness of the Jews and the transformation of the Gentiles to the light.
55_marg299: Or he calls the Gentiles stones, and the sense is: do not glory in the seed of the flesh, because those alone are sons of God who are enlightened by grace and raised up within. He says ‘raise up’ pointedly, because Christ took Sara, that is the Church, and by grace raises up sons of Abraham, Abraham having died without children, lest so great a patriarch be deprived of the promises. As a presage of this thing, God of old begot a son of Sara.
55_interl218: And if you be Christ’s, then are you the seed of Abraham
55_marg300: But lest they seem exempt if they separate themselves from such sacraments, he threatens.
55_marg301: Christ, who consists of a handle and iron, that is, of the humanity by which he is held and of the divinity by which he cuts. It is laid, because although he waits in patience, yet he sees what he is going to do. To the root, that is, to the end of the Jewish people, so that he may take away from the land of the living those who do not believe in Christ. Or the axe is the sentence of judgment, or the preaching of the gospel.
55_marg302: Note: not to the branches, but to the root. For when the sons of evil are taken away, what else is it than the branches of an unfruitful tree being cut off? When the whole offspring is taken away together with the parent, the tree is cut off at the root, so that nothing remains from which a shoot may spring again.
55_marg303: The roots are the thoughts by which they are planted, which either are raised up to heaven or sent down to the depths of hell.
55_marg304: The tree is ‘the human race’. Of its branches, some are dry, that is pagans, fit for burning. Others are green but without fruit, like hypocrites who put forward the appearance of holiness but are empty within. Others are fruitful but poisonous, that is heretics, who by preaching bear fruit that is deadly. Others, that is Catholics, bear good fruit. “Every tree therefore that doth not yield good fruit, shall be cut down, and cast into the fire”: so the Gentiles; the hypocrites, who bear none; and the heretics, who bear evil.
55_interl221: He returns to himself, defining the manner of his baptism.
55_marg305: “I indeed, etc.” Lest he seem to threaten by his own authority, he begins to reveal how great is the dignity of him whose presence he threatens, or by whose benefits he persuades.
55_marg306: That is, I only wash bodies, because I cannot loose sins; so that, as by birth I go before by preaching, so by baptizing I may direct to the baptism of Christ the penitents whom I distinguish from the impenitent by this sign.
55_marg307: And if I admonish you to bring forth worthy fruits of penance, to cast off pride, yet I cannot loose you from sins.
55_marg308: Because I baptize into penance, he into remission. I have the Spirit, he gives it. I preach the kingdom of heaven, he gives it.
55_marg309: “Whose shoes I am not worthy to bear.” Others write: “the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to loose.” John could say either, whether in one continuous speech or at different times, so that one evangelist took up this and another that. All, however, told the truth. He intends in this to show the excellence of Christ and his own humility.
55_marg310: Or, according to allegory, the shoe is the mystery of the incarnation, and the strap the binding of the mystery. John therefore is not able to loose the strap, because he does not suffice to investigate the mystery of the incarnation.
55_marg311: Or: “I am not worthy to loose the latchet of his shoes”: that is, I do not usurp to myself the name of the bridegroom, nor do I wish to be believed or called the bridegroom, but I wish to be the friend of the bridegroom. For it was the custom that if someone was unwilling to take in marriage her who belonged to him, the one who approached her as bridegroom by right of kinship would loose his shoe. John therefore, who is not the bridegroom, says: “I am not worthy to loose the latchet of the shoes”, as if to say: I cannot uncover the footprints of the Redeemer, because I do not usurp to myself the name of bridegroom.
55_marg312: Or he humbles himself simply; or he is not worthy to carry about by preaching the sacraments of the gospel, which was not assigned to him but committed to the apostles.
55_marg313: I am not worthy to explain the nature of divinity to humanity. Or I am not worthy to bear the preaching of the gospel, or to usurp the name of bridegroom.
55_marg314: John, as a pure man, could not give the Spirit by which sin is forgiven. Christ, however, gives it, because he is God and baptizes in the word, of which it is said: “Now you are clean by reason of the word, which I have spoken to you”, and elsewhere: “cleansing it by the laver of water in the word of life.”
55_interl225: because he sanctifies from sins and kindles the love of God
55_marg315: IN THE HOLY GHOST, or the Spirit of sanctification. And in fire, that is, the proof of tribulation. Or, the Spirit washes in the present; afterwards, if any stain creeps in, he will burn it clean with purgatorial fire, which is to be believed of lighter sins. Whence in Leviticus, upon the altar, fire sent from heaven always burned, that is, the fire of divine love, which as it were rebaptizes all in Christ, that is, all who are offered upon the altar, and burns up the vices of their flesh.
55_interl226: by tribulation or by purgatorial fire
55_interl227: that is, the discernment of judgment
55_interl228: those who do not believe are not removed by this fan, because they are already judged
55_marg316: The fan in hand is the examination of judgment, by which the light and the empty are separated from the fruit of good work.
55_marg317: “In his hand”, because: “neither doth the Father judge any man, but hath given all judgment to the Son.”
55_marg318: That is, he cleanses daily from various temptations. Or he will thoroughly cleanse when, because of manifest sins, the perverse one is cast out of the Church; or after death he is condemned.
55_interl232: steadfast in hope of eternal things
55_marg319: Chaff is of the same origin from which wheat also arises, that is, from the seed; but tares are of a different one. So the chaff are those who are imbued with the sacraments of faith but are not solid. The tares, however, are separated from the elect both by work and by profession. Of these it is said: “He that doth not believe is already judged”, and therefore no mention is made here of them.
55_marg320: “Unquenchable”, because it will not be quenched, nor will it quench the tormented, but will punish eternally. It is said, however, in contrast to that of which it is said: “Thou hast tried us by fire,” etc.
55_interl235: that he who had long been hidden might be made manifest
55_marg321: When John was preaching and baptizing, namely when Jesus was thirty years old, showing that no priest or preacher ought to be made except of mature age. As Joseph at thirty received the kingdom of Egypt, and David began his reign at that age; Ezechiel merited prophecy.
55_marg322: Jesus came for these reasons: to approve John’s baptism; and so that, since he was a man, he might fulfill all justice and the humility of the law; and that, sanctifying the waters through the dove in the laver, he might show the coming of the Holy Ghost. For he came not from any need of washing, but so that no one, however holy, might judge the grace of baptism superfluous.
55_interl236: because he had dwelt in Nazareth
55_interl237: because in it the figure of baptism went before, and from its name it demands a descent from pride
55_marg323: Galilee: transmigration; Jordan: descent. Therefore whoever wishes to be baptized should migrate from vices, and, descending, be humbled.
55_interl239: the Lord by a servant; let no one therefore disdain one who is lower
55_interl240: a soldier imitates the king’s humility
55_interl244: to be cleansed from original sin, because you are: “the Lamb of God, who taketh away the sins of the world”
55_interl246: that that for which I came be fulfilled
55_marg324: Suffer me now to be baptized by you, so that afterwards what you seek from me, you may be baptized in the Spirit. For thus it is fitting that we give an example of fulfilling all justice, so that all may learn that no one is perfect without the water of baptism.
55_interl247: adds why he comes to be baptized
55_interl248: because my life is the discipline of morals
55_interl249: so, that is, while I, superior and needing nothing, am regarded by you
55_interl250: to teach the fulfilment of justice, that is, to invite to baptism, because baptism is the fulfilment of all justice
55_interl251: I by receiving, you by baptizing
55_marg325: Thus, that is, by the example of humility, to lead back to life and to show that no one is perfectly just without baptism. For if I, who was born of the Holy Ghost, do not disdain it, how much more necessary is it that others, though just, be baptized even by lesser ones? Hence it is fitting that all justice be first fulfilled, namely that through which the sum of all justice is afterwards fulfilled by all; so that no one glories from works or from his own will, but, knowing himself guilty, is subject to the justice of God. Therefore whoever is “born again of water and the Holy Ghost” is called just, because he fulfills that through which all justice is fulfilled by grace; which it was fitting first for Christ to fulfill, not from need but from mystery, so that he, reborn as Son of God, might make all reborn sons of God his brothers.
55_marg326: Thus, that is, by submitting to a servant and an inferior. All justice, that is, humility, which is all justice. And perfect humility has three degrees. The first is to submit oneself to a greater and not to prefer oneself to an equal; this is called ‘sufficient’, because it suffices that someone be humbled thus, and this degree is necessary for every just man. The second degree is to submit oneself to an equal and not to prefer oneself to a lesser; this is called ‘abundant’. The third is to be subject to a lesser, and in this is all justice. Christ fulfilled this, who has only one part, because it consists in unity and is perfected. Others are distinguished in two ways, because the less perfect are not thus heaped up into unity.
55_marg327: Having thus recognized that justice was to be fulfilled in such an order, he yielded, because true humility is, whose companion obedience does not desert.
55_marg328: The Spirit in a moment taught him what he had not known before; and so, instructed, he humbly fulfilled what he had previously feared.
55_interl255: because those baptized ought to ascend to the homeland through virtues
55_interl256: which is the foundation of the ascent
55_marg329: BAPTIZED, moreover, etc. Christ sanctified the waters of baptism, because to whom it belongs to create, to the same belongs to sanctify.
55_marg330: As a man consists of two, that is body and soul, so he is reborn of two: water, which cleanses filth and buries together with Christ, and the fire of the Spirit, by which, being set aflame, we are caught up to heaven. Thus the Church after baptism seeks the summit of virtues by certain increments, as Christ, baptized, ascended out of the water. Her children ascend after baptism, because they advance to virtues; and those who were first carnal and sons of Adam become spiritual and sons of God.
55_marg331: Thus the Church after baptism seeks the summit of virtues by certain increments.
55_marg332: And this is for the fulfilment of justice. For the heavens were not then first opened to him, nor was the Holy Ghost then first given; but he showed that by the baptism received the way to heaven is opened to us, and the Holy Ghost is given. For that the heavens were opened, that the Holy Ghost came, that the voice of the Father sounded, etc., these are mystical in us.
55_marg333: The way to heaven, which was closed through Adam, is opened for the reborn through Christ.
55_interl257: Jesus saw it, and the Baptist, as John says
55_interl258: the Spirit in the dove, the Son in the man, the Father in the voice. Thus the presence of the Trinity consecrated baptism
55_marg334: He had a true body, formed for the hour, in the appearance of a dove, because otherwise the Spirit could not be seen by men as a dove; not that it was a true dove, but the Spirit in bodily appearance, yet not itself a body. So this figure is understood as others in which God appeared, which when the office was fulfilled were dissolved.
55_marg335: Well: the Spirit descended in a dove, which is simple and gentle, so that it might show the simplicity of its own nature, and that the one into whom it descended is a gentle herald and giver of mercy. Likewise all who are reborn in baptism ought to be filled with the seven virtues signified in the dove. The dove is alien from the malice of gall, in which we are forbidden anger. It harms no one with beak or talons, in which innocence is noted. Nor does it attack the smallest birds, on whom other birds feed themselves and their young, in which we are forbidden rapine. It feeds on pure grain, in which abstinence is noted. It cherishes others as its own young: behold charity. It gives groaning for song: behold compunction. It sits upon the waters, so that, having foreseen the hawk’s shadow in the waters, it may turn aside: behold care.
55_marg336: In the dove the Spirit appeared over the Lord, because he came to gather us by gentleness; over the disciples in fire, whom he came to kindle to consume the rust of sin against themselves.
55_marg337: So great a splendor surrounded Christ at baptism that the empyrean heaven seemed to be opened.
55_marg338: Adam, by sinning, lost heaven; Christ, glorified by the Holy Ghost in the dove, appeared. The quivering flame that had barred the way, the water of baptism extinguished, because water is contrary to fire.
55_interl260: this voice is not to tell him what he does not know, but to benefit the hearers
55_interl263: He was displeased in Adam; whence: “It repenteth me that I have made man.”
55_marg339: That is, I have established my good pleasure, so that you, in whom nothing but good pleases, and through you others may please, not in themselves but in you, that is, united to you by faith and charity.
55_marg340: The other evangelists: “in thee I am well pleased.” For me, that is, I have established my pleasure in you; this is, to do through you what pleases me.
55_marg341: Then Jesus was led, etc. After baptism, because there is no delay from temptation. So that he may at once teach them to fight in the desert, he teaches the baptized to go out from the world and be at leisure for God in quiet. So the children of Israel, after the crossing of the sea, ascend through the desert and eat manna until they come to the land of promise.
55_marg342: This is for monks and novice clerics, who ought first to be in solitary places and not be placed over worldly affairs, because they can be quickly and easily overthrown; on this account the Apostle says: “Not a neophyte.”
55_marg343: Then Jesus. This is the order of right conduct: that after receiving the grace of the Holy Ghost we gird ourselves more tightly against the devil, and, leaving the age in mind, we hunger for the joys of eternal life as for manna in the desert. There temptation happens, because the enemy does not rise up before man leaves the world; for he holds him under his laws. In the desert one fights with hardships, because Adam, abounding in delights in paradise, was conquered by pleasures.
55_marg344: Historically. In that desert which lies between Jerusalem and Jericho, Christ conquered the devil; where, figuratively, it had been said that Adam fell among robbers and was conquered by them, and that the robbers dwelt there. A place called Domim, that is, blood, proves it, on account of the effusion of blood that happened there. By that way the Samaritan went down, because, clothed in flesh, he endured the same temptations.
55_marg345: The Holy Ghost, who fills those whom he sends into battle, makes them strong. Without this Spirit, whoever goes into battle soon falls.
55_marg346: ‘That’ is not put causally, but consecutively; for he was led into the desert and afterwards tempted.
55_marg347: No one is tempted by the devil unless he has gone out into the desert, that is, has begun to study what is good.
55_interl267: that he fasts is of divine power
55_marg348: He fasts so that he may be tempted; he is tempted because he fasts; and he gives us an example of fasting; and that he fasts is of divine power.
55_marg349: Moses and Elias fasted, but not by power as Christ did: Moses was sustained by the word of God, Elias by the strength of food. Nor are those two said to have hungered; but Christ, as man, hungers, so that God may be hidden; it signifies, moreover, the desire of our salvation.
55_marg350: Behold, it agrees with the law, which is received through Moses, and with the prophets, who came through Elias: forty days are the four parts of the world, from which Christ gathers his own, and the ten precepts of the law, with which he arms his own against the world’s pleasures. He fasts forty days before death, while needing food, as if to say: ‘In the time of struggle, abstain from the desires of the age.’ He eats after the resurrection forty days, not needing food, as if to say: ‘I am your consolation and food all days.’ Whence: “Behold, I am with you all days,” etc. For in the same way, while we walk the way of the Lord, we fast from the vanity of the age, and are refreshed by the promise of what is to come.
55_marg351: In Christ’s battle, first he fights against gluttony, through which the first man was overcome. Gluttony inflames the lusts and feeds the desire of the flesh, which fights against the law of the mind. Unless this is first restrained, labour against the rest is in vain. Forty days: this number designates the whole time in which Christ fights with his own. In this number two laws are fulfilled through abstinence, because in forty the decalogue of commandments and the four gospels resound. Hence it is ordained that we fight more keenly with this number, to wash away the sins that are committed, while through the motion of the flesh charity is violated; and so, as long as we are here, let us weep over sins, because by this number life is shown entirely.
55_interl269: this is added lest it be thought that he ate during the night
55_marg352: This is truly of humanity, and by this there is an occasion for temptation. The power is hidden, the weakness is open.
55_marg353: Because hunger is a sign of weakness. And so in abstinence temptation is not lacking to us. Through outward weakness he tempts Christ, in whom he found no law of sin.
55_interl270: he tests what he fears, and yet he does not hold himself back from tempting him
55_marg354: Of these, one belongs to the tester, another to the tempter, while he seems to confess God and tries to play tricks on man. For he tempts so that he may test what he dreads; he tests so that by tempting he may deceive.
55_marg355: He knew the Son of God had come into the world, whether through the prophets, or through the angels announcing, or through John pointing him out; but because he saw lowly things in him, from which he suspected the deity, from pride it came into doubt for him. Hence he also asks craftily. Nor was it unworthy that Christ, who had come to be killed, should be tempted, so that by overcoming temptations he might give us power to overcome temptations, just as by his death he took away our mortality.
55_marg356: Christ permitted himself to be tempted only after baptism, suggesting that those who come to him would suffer heavier temptations.
55_marg357: He urges that hunger be relieved by bread made from stones, not because he cares for his salvation, but that from the change he may learn his power; even if he were a mere man, bread with its pleasure would mock the hunger of one who suffers it.
55_marg358: Temptation comes about in three ways: by suggestion, by delight, by consent. Christ was indeed tempted only by suggestion, because the delight of sin did not bite his mind.
55_interl271: because he knew it is written: “He spoke, and they were made.”
55_interl273: he began with gluttony; in the order by which he brought down Adam, he is conquered by this same thing
55_interl274: the stone signifies the hardness of the devil
55_interl275: he tempers the answer, lest he recognize him to be God
55_marg359: He does not use power, but the authority of the Scriptures, teaching us to fight by doctrine rather than by miracles.
55_interl276: that is, in the sacramental species, but in the word of life
55_marg360: As if he said: your persuasion is a temptation, because you deal with food of the body and not food of the mind. The lower part of man is sustained by bread, the other is refreshed by the word of God; because you deal with the lower part, it is plain that you are a tempter.
55_interl277: he uses sayings, teaching us that we conquer not by power but by humility
55_interl278: the word of God proceeds from the mouth, because God’s will is related through the Scriptures
55_marg361: Every word is charity, in which all things that proceed from the mouth of God are fulfilled; for whatever ministry they are spoken by, they are not theirs but God’s. But if anything adverse is inserted, that is not of God. From the one Word, that is, the wisdom of God, proceeds whatever the saints speak, who are his mouth.
55_interl280: historically this temptation was the last
55_marg362: The first and last temptation were in the desert; the middle also, historically. The last was after he had returned to Jerusalem, because Matthew follows not the order of history but the temptation of Adam; Luke, as the thing was done.
55_marg363: Because, overcome by Christ’s answer and left uncertain, after the first he came to the second temptation.
55_marg364: That he permitted himself to be taken up was not weakness but patience. In the devil, however, it was not virtue but pride.
55_marg365: Note that all these things were accomplished through the bodily senses. Nor is it surprising if he permitted himself to be carried about, if the taking up is understood thus, he who permitted himself to be crucified.
55_interl281: by permission, not by weakness; hence the enemy grows proud
55_interl282: Jerusalem, where the temple was and the worship of God was
55_marg366: In Palestine the roofs were flat on top, and there was the seat of teachers from which they spoke to the people; there vainglory, puffed up by the honour of teaching, captured many.
55_marg367: In that very place he tempts Christ, where he had deceived many. But while he does not consent, he teaches those who are on high not to be moved by empty glory.
55_marg368: The devil seeks heights; he always leads to heights, lifting up through boasting, so that he may be able to cast down.
55_marg369: In that Christ permitted himself to be lifted up on high, but did not obey the one urging him to fall, he shows that we should obey whoever commands good and high things, but resist him who wants to cast us down.
55_interl285: no place dedicated to God restrains him
55_interl286: temptation from empty glory, like Adam, to whom he said: “You shall be as gods.”
55_marg370: In all temptations he does this, so that he may learn whether he is the Son of God. But Christ tempers his answer so that he leaves it ambiguous.
55_marg371: Because the words are exchanged with one another, it is likely that the devil appeared in the form of a man.
55_marg372: This voice fits him who strives to cast all men down. In it he is shown to be weak, that he can harm no one unless he himself first casts himself down.
55_marg373: For he suggested that by some sign he might test how much power he has with God. But no one ought to tempt God when he has from human reason what to do. Hence, although he could do all things, he said to his own: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another.” And he himself fled and departed and hid. Now too he could come down from the temple otherwise than by casting himself down through boasting. When human reason fails, let a man commend himself to God, not by tempting but by devoutly trusting.
55_interl287: he uses the Scriptures not to set up virtues but to thrust in errors, as his own also do
55_interl288: he who goes against the stronger provides him with an occasion of victory
55_marg374: “That he hath given his angels charge over thee,” etc. Bede. What is well said of the body, the devil interprets badly of the head. For if he says this of Christ, why not also that which is said there against him: “Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk: and thou shalt trample under foot the lion and the dragon”? But he speaks of the help of angels as to one who is weak, and is silent about his own trampling.
55_interl289: the law written on stone tablets, in which all stumbled
55_interl291: in Deuteronomy, from which he therefore brings forward testimonies, in order to confirm the mysteries of the second law
55_interl292: although conquered, yet he does not cease
55_marg375: Again he took him, etc. This temptation came first in order, but is related out of order according to what happened to Adam.
55_interl293: upon the mountain of pride every covetous man is raised up
55_marg376: Isidore. This mountain signifies pride, by which he fell and makes others fall. Exceedingly high, because he wanted to draw him to the summit of pride.
55_marg377: About to tempt from covetousness, he led him up a mountain, because covetousness and ambition always seek the heights.
55_interl295: because all things are momentary; not that the devil, but divine power, could do this
55_marg378: He showed, etc. Not that he enlarged the sight of him who sees all, but by showing the vanity of worldly pomp, which he loved as if it were beautiful, he wanted to make him love it. Or the devil, knowing that Christ would take the kingdom from him, showed him all the kingdoms of the world, not the Persians or Medes, but how he would reign among worldly men. Or through gluttony, or through covetousness, or through other things, so that by persuading him he might subject him to himself. Luke says: “In a moment” all things were shown to him, in which not so much the speed of the sight as the frail fragility of the power is expressed.
55_marg379: God showed Moses in a moment the whole land of promise by the power of his deity; so it was done now.
55_marg380: He showed him all the kingdoms, that is, the parts of the earth in which each kingdom was situated. Just as if some should say, pointing at the mountains: “Behold, there is Rome,” not showing the city itself, but the part of the earth in which it is situated.
55_marg381: All the desirable things in the world in which men reign. Or simply, the whole world was seen from the mountain at his suggestion.
55_interl296: how great is his glory in drawing men to vices
55_marg382: Rabanus. Not that he looked upon it with the eye of concupiscence as we do, but this showing was in his mind, as doctors see diseases without injury.
55_interl298: not that he is able to do this
55_marg383: He says this from arrogance, not that the whole world is his.
55_marg384: From the beginning the devil laboured to usurp for himself what belonged to God. Hence, that he might be worshipped in them, he invented idols.
55_marg385: In these three are noted gluttony, covetousness, pride.
55_marg386: Rabanus. Luke places covetousness in the middle and pride last, according to the custom of the present time, because pride rages after all the virtues. In these three, gluttony, covetousness, pride, all the vices joined to them are destroyed. Conquered in gluttony, he does not tempt about lust or the others that arise from gluttony. So also in all others that are in the world, the devil uses them as weapons against us. For nothing in the world is except the concupiscence of the flesh, and the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life. In these three all kinds of temptations are comprehended.
55_interl301: what it would be to fall
55_interl303: from the power which you had before
55_interl305: who is the adversary of salvation
55_marg387: David struck down Goliath with three stones from the torrent, and Christ struck the devil with three testimonies from the law.
55_interl308: not I you, but you ought to adore me as God
55_interl309: by obligation: to whom alone this is owed
55_marg388: This is said either to the devil, not because he will fulfil it from devotion, but so that, contrary to what he was attempting, it may be shown in writing that not he but God is to be adored. Or it is intimated not to the devil but to himself according to his humanity, and to every man, that this precept is given; similarly also that: “Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.”
55_marg389: The Lord God, namely the Son and the Father and the Holy Ghost, who is one God. God is adored, and is served specially for his own sake.
55_marg390: Here it is shown that the man Christ, as God and Lord, is to be adored by obligation.
55_marg391: In Greek it is called latreosis, in Latin servitude. Common servitude, which is called dulia in Greek, is owed to God and to man and to anyone; but that which is due to God alone is distinctly called ‘latria’; hence ‘idolatry,’ which gives to idols what is due to God alone.
55_marg392: Note that the devil is overcome in those things in which he overcame Adam. Whom he tempted from gluttony, when he asked him to taste of the forbidden tree; from vainglory, when he said: “You shall be as Gods”; from covetousness, when he said: “Knowing good and evil.”
55_interl312: “For a time,” as Luke says; he was going to fight later through the Jews
55_interl313: no longer finding what he should do
55_interl315: so that the divinity of the victor may be proved
55_marg393: Not as if approaching then for the first time, but looking from afar at the Lord’s struggle, lest he seem to have needed their protection or to have conquered by it. But when that one, conquered, had departed, they came, ready for service. As in this struggle our warfare is prepared, so in the service of the angels a glorious reward is taught.
55_marg394: CUM AUTEM AUDISSET etc. Here Matthew, like Mark and Luke, passes over the first coming of the Lord into Galilee, after he was baptized, where he changed water into wine, and remained with his mother and disciples at Capharnaum, from which he went up to Jerusalem because of the Passover. Thence he came into Judea and baptized, when John was baptizing in Aenon near Salim. But after John was delivered up, he went again into Galilee. When the Pharisees heard that he baptized and made more disciples than John had made, from this return the three evangelists begin. But John, having tested the gospel of the others for the truth of what was said, saw that some things were lacking, and especially those which Jesus had done in the first year of his preaching; at the request of his brothers he wrote a gospel that the others had passed over before the delivering up of John, gathering, namely, the deeds of one year, in which he also suffered after the prison of John. Hence he also says: “This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee.” And again: “For John was not yet cast into prison.”
55_marg395: This was on account of the gospel. Jesus, preaching the same more perfectly, for a time withdraws and flees, so that he may be an example to his own.
55_marg396: There are two Galilees: one is called that of the Jews, the other of the Gentiles, on account of the dwelling of Gentiles, which part Solomon gave to the king of Tyre, who placed Gentiles there.
55_marg397: Hence Christ is called ‘Nazarene.’ Nazareth is a village in Galilee near Mount Thabor. Capharnaum, a town in Galilee of the Gentiles, situated near the lake of Genesareth, in the land of Zabulon and Nephthalim, where was the first captivity of the Hebrews by the Assyrians. Where therefore was the first forgetting of the law, there is the first preaching of the gospel, so that from a place as it were central it might flow both to the Gentiles and to the Jews.
55_marg398: Allegorically. That leaving Nazareth he passes to Capharnaum shows that he teaches us to pass from the flower of the figures of the law to the fruit of the spiritual things that are in the gospel. But these spiritual things are in a most beautiful town, that is, in the Church, which is maritime, because it is placed near the waves of the age and is daily beaten, and it captures with the nets of the gospel men entangled in the allurements of the world. But it is situated in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim, because it stands firmly in the midst of the Gentiles to spread the word of God, so that it may show a refuge to believers and a harbour of faith to those in danger.
55_interl320: Zabulon, which is in Galilee of the Jews, as Nephthalim is of the Gentiles
55_marg399: Zabulon: dwelling of strength. Nephthalim: enlargement.
55_marg400: In these tribes were small villages from which the apostles came. Whence: “The princes of Zabulon, the princes of Nephthali.”
55_marg401: The land of Zabulon, etc. Rabanus. The evangelist passes over what is put first, namely: “At the first time the land of Zabulon and the land of Nephtali was lightly touched”; as also what is in the middle, namely, at the last, “the way of the sea” was heavily loaded. He does this because he intends to show the beginning of Christ’s preaching, and so touches on what is mystical.
55_interl324: which is by the sea and is beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles; namely the people who walked, or the people saw the light, etc.
55_marg402: The way of the sea, etc. The Church, which is by the sea of the age, is itself beyond the Jordan, that is, drawn out through baptism from its former errors. Galilee, that is, a passing over has been made, and what before dwelt under Gentile rite in the shadow of death and the luxury of the flesh is enlightened through faith in Christ, Christ preaching.
55_marg403: Galilee of the Gentiles, which is in the tribe of Neptalim, near the Tyrians, is so called to distinguish it from that Galilee which is in the tribe of Zabulon, which is near Tiberias. In the one that is called ‘of the Gentiles,’ Solomon gave twenty cities to Hiram, king of Tyre, in the lot of the tribe of Neptalim. Christ dwelt in both; but for the figure of those who are to be called from the Gentiles, the one that is of the Gentiles is recorded here.
55_marg404: Augustine. This people, which was first led into captivity and was in the darkness of vices, first saw the light of Christ’s preaching. Then the gospel was spread among all nations. Whence it follows: “to them that sat in the region of the shadow of death,” etc.
55_interl325: is above all to be received in the mystical sense
55_interl326: heard the preaching and the miracles of Christ
55_marg405: Death is in hell; the shadows of this death are sins, which are never without death. Therefore whoever wants to flee death, let him avoid the shadow.
55_interl328: the knowledge of the truth, or the preaching of Christ
55_marg406: From that time, etc. After he was baptized. Baptism makes men fit for preaching.
55_marg407: From that time, that is, after John was delivered up, because when the law ceases the gospel follows, as the sun follows the dawn. A humble master, who does not hinder the teaching of the disciple but waits until he completes his course. In this he teaches that no one should despise a sermon because of a lowly person. Whence the Apostle: “If any thing be revealed to another, let the first hold his peace.”
55_interl329: the voice being emptied out, the Word itself comes
55_interl330: the preaching of disciple and master in harmony
55_interl331: penance is the correction of the evil mind
55_marg408: The same things the herald preaches, so that it may be shown that he is none other than the one who had cried out in the voice. For Christ himself is the Word that cries out in John as the instrument, and in all who from the beginning spoke anything divinely; and yet this one alone is called the voice, because through him the present Word is shown, which the others announced from afar. For between voice and word there is nothing intermediate; but as soon as the voice has sounded, the word is perceived at once. As John, shut up, ceased, Christ shone forth in his powers. Whence John is the figure of the prophets and of the law, who truly are the voice of the crying wisdom of God; of whom John is the end. When these cease, the word that had sounded in them alone is shown by itself.
55_marg409: This preaching of Christ, begun in Capharnaum with dazzling miracles, is said to have begun a year after baptism; or, according to others, it began on the Kalends of May, so that in the same year he was baptized and fasted, and with some days interposed, in which he did the things John wrote. After the Baptist was imprisoned, he began to preach.
55_interl332: that is, Christ, who gives it, or the Church, to whom it is promised and prepared
55_interl333: before these things were said, and therefore he does not add ‘then,’ or ‘next,’ or ‘perhaps,’ after these things were said
55_interl334: the same is called ‘the lake of Genesareth,’ ‘the sea of Tiberias,’ ‘the lake of salt pits’
55_marg410: because he proved the unity of brotherly love, without which no one is admitted into the order of preachers
55_interl335: which is interpreted ‘obedient’; he was called when Andrew led him to Jesus
55_marg411: WHO IS CALLED PETER. Or when Andrew first brought him. This name was given him when it is said: “Thou shalt be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter”; although here it seems to promise for the future. Or when he confessed: “Thou art Christ the Son of the living God,” it was said to him: “Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church.”
55_marg412: Peter ‘recognizing,’ Andrew ‘manly,’ which befits teachers, because these alone are fit for teaching who are illumined by the light of wisdom, and obey God’s precepts, and manfully suggest to others.
55_marg413: He rightly puts first Peter, who is called ‘obedient,’ and Andrew, who is called ‘strong’; because without obedience no one enters, and without strength no one perseveres. And these virtues are kin, because the first man went out disobedient, and the second entered obedient.
55_marg414: Matthew says that he called the disciples after his dwelling in Capharnaum. John says that after water was changed into wine, Jesus came to Capharnaum with his mother and brothers and disciples. But it is uncertain whether they had already attached themselves, so that here, by recapitulation, it is told as if done before; or they are called ‘disciples’ because they went down with him, not because they were then disciples, but because they were to be. Before Jesus came into Cana of Galilee, Andrew had brought Peter, but they were not yet disciples.
55_interl338: intent on the gains of present life
55_marg415: Because those whom he often sees gaping for earthly gains, he calls to heavenly desires; and through them, with the nets of the gospel, he snatches others from the depths of iniquity. 55_marg418: The intention is changed, not the fishing; the nets are changed into teaching, desire into love of souls; the sea becomes the age, the ship the Church, the fish good and bad men.

55_marg421: It is asked how Matthew and Mark say that Jesus called two by two: first Peter and Andrew, afterwards James and John; whereas Luke says that in the great catch of fish, the companions of Peter and Andrew, James and John, were called, when they could not draw the nets, and Jesus finally said to Peter: “Fear not: from henceforth thou shalt catch men,” and at the same time those, having brought the ships to land, followed him. But what Luke says happened first; nor were they then called by the Lord, but only it was foretold to Peter that he would catch men, not that he would afterwards catch no fish. Hence he also says: “having brought their ships to land,” as if with the care of returning. But afterwards, as Matthew and Mark say, two were called, and ordered to follow. Moreover, he sent unlettered fishermen to preach, so that the faith might be thought to be in the power of God, not in the eloquence of men.
55_marg422: Zebedee ‘fugitive,’ that is, ‘the devil.’ James ‘supplanter,’ who is helped by John, that is, by ‘the grace of God.’

55_marg431: Fame is necessary on account of the neighbour, and especially for preachers. This fame follows the aforesaid good works.
55_marg432: His fame went out into all Syria, that is, his renown into all Syria. Syria is every region from the Euphrates to the great sea, from Cappadocia into Egypt, in which is the province of Palestine, where the Jews dwell. Syria is interpreted ‘lofty,’ Galilee ‘rolling’ or ‘turning,’ that is, the world, which is both proud and always turns toward the depths. In it the fame of Christ became known through the preaching of the apostles, through whom the demoniacs were saved, that is, idolaters; the lunatics, that is, the unstable; the paralytics, that is, the slack and torpid. Paralysis in Greek, in Latin, is ‘dissolution.’
55_marg433: Up to the summit of true praise, through the increase of good work. It befitted the master of the pontiffs to have testimony of praise from those who are outside; whence the infirmities of morals are more freely laid open to such.
55_marg434: Allegorically: the demoniacs are idolaters; the lunatics, the unstable; the paralytics, the dissolute and flowing. He speaks of those lunatics whose sickness grows in the waxing of the moon; not that this madness comes from the moon, but the devil, who causes the madness, observes the lunar times, so that he may defame the creature into blasphemy against the Creator.
55_marg435: Among these were some of whom Mark and Luke treat more fully.
55_marg436: He cures bodies, so that they may the more readily hear invisible things. Otherwise it would have been of little account to give care to those who were about to die at once.
55_marg437: They followed, etc. The crowds came in four kinds: namely, some because of the heavenly mystery, like disciples; others for the cure of infirmities; others, wanting to test by mere fame and curiosity whether what was said was true; others, through envy, wanting to accuse him and catch him in something.

55_marg438: Luke agrees with this, saying: “And it came to pass in those days, that he went out into a mountain to pray, and he passed the whole night in the prayer of God. And when day was come, he called unto him his disciples; and he chose twelve of them (whom also he named apostles).” But Luke says that after the descent from the mountain, in a level place, he preached the same sermon to the crowds, standing, which Matthew says was given on the mountain to the disciples, sitting. It may be that on the mountain he chose the twelve, which Matthew is silent about and Luke says; and to the chosen he then gave that discourse which Matthew says and Luke passes over. And after he came down and made another similar discourse to the crowds, which Matthew is silent about, Luke tells it. Or the Lord could first have been with the disciples alone on the height of the mountain, when from them he chose the twelve; then have come down with them to some level place, which nonetheless would be on the mountain and could hold many crowds, and there stood until the crowds gathered; and afterwards, when he had sat down, the disciples came nearer, and so he had one discourse for them and for the others, which Matthew and Luke tell in a different order of narration, but with the same truth of things.
55_marg439: The crowd that followed did not go up; hence another sermon is given to them on the plain. For not all can do all things, which is the truer view, although the same sermon may be seen to have been given to both at once.

55_marg441: The mountain itself ascends into the mountain, so that he might teach the higher summits of virtues, and show that the Church, upon which he sits, preaching the Lord’s precept, is to be raised more sublimely, which the same doctrine would more fully teach until the end of the age. He leads the apostles up more eminently, so that from the mountain the mountains may first receive peace for the people.
55_interl367: the dignity of the teacher’s office is noted
55_interl368: sitting is the incarnation, in which he teaches

55_interl372: signifies that he is about to speak many and great things

55_marg444: The opening of the mouth signifies the depth of the sacrament. As if he had opened an abyss, as if a treasure, as if a river of paradise. On this mountain he writes the New Testament in the hearts of the sons, beginning from the beatitudes; he who on Mount Sinai gave the Old Testament on stones to servants, beginning from terror.
55_interl375: not only by word, but writing within in the heart, as God; now as true man, who before opened the mouths of the prophets
55_marg445: The number of the sentences must be carefully attended to. For the beatitude begins from humility: “Blessed are the poor in spirit”; and in the seventh is wisdom, that is, contemplation of truth, pacifying the whole man, receiving the likeness of God: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.” The eighth returns to the head, because it shows consummation. In the first and the eighth, therefore, the kingdom of heaven is named. For seven are the things that perfect, the eighth brightens, and shows what is perfect. To these seven degrees corresponds the sevenfold operation of the Holy Ghost, which Isaias describes. But he begins from the highest, this one from the lowest: because there the Son of God is taught as about to descend to the depths, here man, from the depths, is about to ascend to the likeness of God. In these, the first is fear, which here suits humble men, of whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor”; that is, not puffed up, not wise in high things, but fearing. The second is piety, which belongs to the meek. For he who piously seeks honours holy things, does not rebuke, does not resist, which is to become meek. The third is knowledge, which belongs to those who mourn, who have learned by what evils they are now bound, and have sought what are as it were goods. The fourth is fortitude, which belongs to those who hunger and thirst, because desiring joy they labour for true goods, wishing to be turned away from earthly things. The fifth is counsel, which belongs to the merciful, because one remedy for being delivered from such great evils is to forgive others and to lend to them as we wish to be done to us. The sixth is understanding, which belongs to the clean of heart, who with a purged eye can see what the eye does not see. The seventh is patience, which belongs to the peacemakers, in whom there is no motion, nothing rebellious, but all things obey the spirit. One reward is named in different ways according to the fitness of each. To the poor: the kingdom of heaven, which is of perfect wisdom, as if it were said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” To the meek: an inheritance, as the father’s testament to those who seek with piety. To those who mourn: consolation, as to those who know by what they are plunged. To those who hunger and thirst: satiety, as refreshment to those who strive and labour. To the merciful: the mercy they bestow on others. To the clean of heart: the vision of God, as by a purged eye. To the peacemakers: the likeness of God, as to those formed to the image of God.
55_marg446: Each of these beatitudes, that it may be fulfilled, asks the help of the seven gifts; and that these gifts may be had, we pray in the Lord’s Prayer with seven petitions. Behold how the wisdom of God foresaw all things: the virtue of the beatitudes is received from the gift of the Holy Ghost; the gift is obtained by the petition of the prayer which Christ composed.
55_marg447: Indeed there are seven gifts, but one Spirit; seven petitions, but one prayer: “One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek after.” Seven beatitudes of virtues, one charity.
55_marg448: Blessed are the poor in spirit. Because it is not necessity but faith and devotion of poverty that makes them blessed, so that, all things despised, they live for God. This has two parts: the renunciation of things, and the breaking of the spirit, so that even the good man counts himself useless and inferior to others. The beatitude is already in the hope of attaining it.
55_marg449: Poor in spirit are those who have all things and possess nothing.
55_marg450: The poor in spirit is one who is humble in heart, having a poor spirit; humility is its nurse.
55_marg451: As: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” so poverty is the beginning of blessedness.
55_interl377: in hope, which makes them blessed
55_interl378: to the poor, heavenly riches are fittingly promised in the present
55_interl379: the humble who fear God; whence he rightly begins: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” as: “Pride is the beginning of sin,” by which the kingdom of earth is sought; here, the kingdom of heaven
55_interl380: without harshness of mind and without spite
55_marg452: The meek are those who master bad habits; perfect virtue is the possession of morals.
55_marg453: The meek is one whom the harshness or bitterness of mind does not affect, but the simplicity of faith teaches him to bear every injury patiently.
55_marg454: The meek is one whom neither rancour nor anger affects, but who bears all things with equanimity. In this great virtue the Lord makes himself, as it were, its master, which he would not do unless this virtue were the way of supreme perfection. Whence the Lord: “Learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart.” This virtue possesses the land of the living and delights in the multitude of peace.
55_marg455: The meek man neither provokes nor is provoked; neither harms nor thinks of harming.
55_marg456: Those who yield to the wicked and overcome evil with good, these shall possess the land of the living. The fierce quarrel over earthly things.
55_marg457: A fitting ascent. First is contempt of the world, to which eternal things are given; then meekness and gentleness temper the morals; and no one is meek who was not first poor. For it is impossible to climb to the second step unless you have first grasped the first, because amid riches, cares and hatreds the mind is not meek. But the matter of this fire is scarcely wiped away to purity, and therefore this gentleness is often corrupted or dragged out. Whence it is added: Blessed are they that mourn, for their own or others’ sins, which mourning is from the lower watering; but that which comes from the upper watering is from desire for the heavenly fatherland; the former washes away present filth, the latter kindles more keenly the lovers of eternal things. He who has laid down sins and corrected his morals by meekness, and has also wept, can now hunger and thirst for justice, which before he could not. This virtue is not fulfilled without the spirit of fortitude, because through it, hungering, we shall at last come to satiety.
55_interl381: of the living, for steadfastness and firmness
55_interl382: for their own sins and those of others. Having scorned the world, with a pure desire for heaven
55_marg458: It remains, after the aforesaid flood of ruins, to cleanse by mourning. Mourning for sins, or for the heavenly desire, merits consolation, and no other.
55_marg459: These are illumined by the spirit of knowledge, that they may know by what evils they are entangled.
55_interl383: by the Spirit Paraclete, of eternal joy
55_interl384: on account of the blessed consolation
55_interl385: they shall hunger for justice; they are strengthened by the Spirit of fortitude
55_marg460: Lovers of the true good, to whom it is not enough that they are just, but who always thirst for the work of justice.

55_marg461: Justice is to render to each his own: to himself, to neighbours and to God. This justice will not be fully fulfilled until “God may be all in all.” Therefore here we can hunger, but not be satisfied.
55_marg462: Mercy is the light of justice; justice is the strength of mercy. This mercy needs the spirit of counsel, without which no one shows mercy circumspectly. The beginning is to show mercy to oneself; the end is to die for another. For the order of mercy is that each one begin with himself; Christ indicates the end, having died for sinners out of mercy.
55_interl387: when they have obtained what they desire
55_interl388: those who help others in any way, to whom this is repaid by God, that they may be freed from misery
55_interl389: mercy is to give and to forgive
55_marg463: Mercy is born from what goes before: for if true humility has gone first, and the mind becomes meek, and mourns its own and others’ falls, and hungers for justice, then true mercy is born afterwards. For then he will make others’ miseries his own, and will help as far as his powers allow; and if the ability to help is lacking, compassion will not be lacking. Of this it is said: “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful”; that is, be merciful to this end to which God also is, that goodness may overflow in all.
55_marg464: Mercy without justice is called ‘remissness’ and ‘lukewarmness’; justice without mercy is called ‘severity’ and ‘austerity’.
55_interl390: judgment without mercy will be done to him who would not show mercy
