55_marg465: Purity of heart is placed sixth, so that man, created on the sixth day, may be restored through it, and, with vices driven away, the precept of the Lord may enlighten the eyes so that God can be seen. Therefore, the five degrees having been passed, the eye of the mind must be cleansed, lest the soul, offended in one of the commandments, become guilty of all. Therefore man should strip himself of the world, love eternal things, and embrace God, until he can see him whom he sees only so far as he dies to the age. In the future he will be seen as he is by the eye of the mind. Therefore the spirit of understanding is fitted to this degree, because understanding is the eye of the mind, and the fulfilling of God’s commandments opens understanding.
55_interl392: here by hope, there by the thing itself
55_marg466: Rabanus. The peacemakers are those who settle all movements of the soul and subject them to reason, because nothing opposes those who are like their Father, who is supreme rest. He is raised upright who rules over the perverse, with this peace firmly established within; whatever he stirs up within, he who is cast out outwardly increases glory, and when it fails, it makes known how great the firmness within is. Whence it follows: “Blessed are they that suffer persecution,” etc.
55_marg467: This peace is nourished only by good will. Whence: “And on earth peace to men of good will.” The world cannot give this, but Jesus can, who says: “My peace I give unto you.” This peace surpasses all sense, but is grasped by faith; whence also we are illumined by it, and, reconciled to it, we lead ourselves away from everyone who dissents from it. But when God is all in all, then the blessedness of adoption will be given.
55_marg468: In the present, indeed, a man at peace, though he wages war with vices, in nothing breaks the peace which God gave. Whence: “Much peace have they that love thy law,” etc. But he who is divided from it is a son of wrath. Through it we become sons, beyond which nothing more is promised. In this is wisdom, the greatest of the gifts; according to the increase of virtues there are also increases of rewards, because “another glory of the sun,” etc.
55_marg469: Peace is the only-begotten Son of God, of whom it is said: “For he is our peace.” He who loves peace is a son of peace.
55_marg470: Peace begins with us, because while the law of the flesh resists the law of the mind, we cannot be peacemakers not only toward others but not even toward ourselves. But after the spirit within commands, so that the whole man serves the spirit, then peace flows out to others, so that we may have “peace with all men.” True peace indeed is where nothing resists. The peace of God surpasses all sense; it cannot be grasped as it is, yet it can be grasped according to our capacity, not as great as it is, but as far as is sufficient for the reconciliation of adoption. The infinity of eternal peace, though it cannot be understood, and how peace befits the sons of wrath, and how God, as peace, judges severely, and how great and what kind of peace the whole Trinity is, where there is one power, one operation, yet what it is, and that it is so great and such as it is proclaimed, we grasp by faith. He who is purged attends to and is directed toward the degree of peace.
55_marg471: In the aforesaid seven is perfection; in the eighth, the showing and proof of perfection. Those who have the aforesaid things can suffer persecution, and rightly hold the aforesaid things, which he has received who is prepared to die for them.
55_marg472: Those who ascend through the aforesaid things up to wisdom, being perfected and strengthened, do not yield to persecution, because neither death nor life can separate them from Christ.
55_marg473: Whose minds the exercises of the aforesaid beatitudes illumine, their purity guides the heart to God, so that the image deleted by sin may be reformed.

55_marg474: The eighth saying, which returns to the head and declares the perfect man, also signifies circumcision on the eighth day, and the Lord’s resurrection after the Sabbath, which is the eighth and first day, and the octaves which we celebrate in the New Testament, and the number of Pentecost. For in the number seven multiplied by seven, which makes forty-nine, one is added as an eighth, so that fifty may be completed; and as if one returned to the head, on the day when the Holy Ghost was sent, by which we are led into the kingdom of heaven, and receive the inheritance; we are consoled, and fed, and obtain mercy, and are cleansed, and made peaceful, and so we endure persecutions inflicted from without and molestations for truth and justice. The eighth beatitude, indeed of circumcision, ends in martyrdom, which makes it proven, and is fulfilled by the preceding gifts.
55_marg475: The eighth promise is nothing other than the first repeated in words. There is a mystery in the number that is repeated in the promise. Within the seven it sounds first, and afterwards it is counted outside, so that the glory of resurrection is consecrated by these eight degrees. The eighth is the day of resurrection, which is also the first, the day on which light too was created.
55_marg476: In general the kingdom of heaven is said of all, although a particular number of merits is counted; for although it may rightly be said of him who will be last, yet the dignity of all will be common to all, since through charity what is in others, he who is last also will possess.
55_marg477: “Blessed” is said of one who wills nothing evil and has all that he wills. And therefore everyone there is blessed, because he does not will more, since he wills nothing unjustly.
55_marg478: Up to here he has set out the sayings generally, as if to the absent, though they pertain also to those present; now he turns his words to them, although this too belongs to others, foretelling how much they were about to suffer for his name, because he wished to make known to them the dignity of their rank, saying: “You are the salt of the earth,” “You are the light of the world,” so that from sorrow they might receive humility, and from joys consolation.
55_marg479: As Moses, setting out the ten precepts, afterwards explains them part by part, so Christ sets out the eight beatitudes as kinds of virtue, from which all that the Lord said on the mount depends. But because he had concluded many things obscurely in few words, he explains more broadly. Whence he pursues more broadly the parts of persecutions about the eighth beatitude, expressing especially that the apostles and their followers were about to suffer for justice.
55_marg480: The old translation has: ‘When men shall hate you, and shall say all that is evil, and shall cast you out.’ The sense is the same in ours, since evil words are spoken out of hatred of heart.
55_marg481: He who desires the glory of heaven does not fear reproach on earth. As much as each rejoices in the praise of men, so much is he crestfallen at reproach. He whom praise lifts up, blame casts down. Where one seeks to be praised only before God, he does not fear to be confounded in the sight of men.

55_marg488: Here now the apostolic office is shown: namely that they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world.
55_marg489: This applies specially to the apostles, who ought to be adorned with the aforesaid virtues, namely poverty and the others, so that they may be the best salt, seasoning others by their teaching and by the example of their life.
55_marg490: Salt is salvation from corruption. Whence the prophet: “I have given thee to be the light of the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation even to the farthest part of the earth.”
55_marg491: Where the corruption of guilt is dried up by the salt of wisdom, the worms do not destroy it.
55_marg492: “You are” etc. Because the earth, that is human nature, is seasoned through them with the wisdom of the Word. Salt makes the land barren; whence in the anger of the victors they sowed salt in the destroyed cities, so that no sprout might arise in them. So the apostles, the kingdom of sin being destroyed, suppressed the sprouting of vices. Salt seasons foods and dries meats; but preaching preserves human nature unharmed for its Creator from worms and the putrefaction of vices. As food is not savoury unless seasoned with salt, so speech is not useful without the teaching of apostolic doctrine. Whence in Leviticus: “Every oblation of thine shalt thou season with salt”; that is, in everything you say or do, have apostolic wisdom. Salt is made of water and fire; so these are born from the water of the Holy Ghost and the fire of tribulation. Or through the water of baptism and the fire of charity they are born to the savour of wisdom.
55_interl411: that is, if the teacher has erred
55_marg493: “But if the salt” etc. That is, if you, by whom others are to be seasoned, give way to adversity or prosperity, by whom will the error be removed from you, when God has chosen to take you away and set others in your place? It is worth nothing, because (as another evangelist says) it is neither fit for the land, which it prevents from sprouting by its contact, nor for the dunghill, which it does not allow to fertilize. So he who goes back neither bears fruit himself nor is able to cultivate others, but is cast out by the Church, and is mocked in these words: “This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
55_marg494: That is, if the teacher, through fear or desire, has let the savour of wisdom slip away, by whom will his folly be corrected? This belongs only to the apostles; what follows applies to all masters: “It is good for nothing any more,” etc. In the end he concludes about all in this way: “Unless your justice abound,” etc.

Whence it is said: “I chastise my body,” etc. Or, Christ lights the lamp, when he filled the earthen vessel of human nature with the flame of his divinity, which he neither hides from believers nor encloses within the bushel, that is, the measure of the law, or the bounds of one nation. 55_marg525: Christ’s addition: not to be angry, not to desire; from these it is hard to abstain, and therefore they are great in reward.
55_marg526: Anger is every evil motion to harm. A sudden motion to which one does not consent is a first emotion (propassio). When consent is added, it is passion, and death in the house.
55_marg527: There are degrees in these sins. First is to be angry and to retain this motion in the mind; it is more if the agitation itself has forced out a voice by which he who is angered is struck; more still if a certain reproach has rebuked. Similarly there are degrees in punishment: for the judgment is less when the case is still being tried with the accused, and there is room for defence. It is more when the judges confer among themselves by what torment they are to condemn one who is agreed to be condemned; more still is gehenna, where there is no delay of sentence. And so what could not be expressed in proper and certain modes has been distinguished by certain likenesses. For by these three, judgment, council, and gehenna, diverse mansions in eternal damnation are signified, according to the measure of sin.
55_marg528: Some add ‘without cause,’ as also in saying ‘raca’ or ‘fool.’ It is natural to be angry, yet so that it is not without cause. To this sense it seems fitting: “Be angry, and sin not.” But every occasion of anger is removed, while we are commanded to love enemies.
55_marg529: He who is not angry does not dissolve the law, but fulfils it, so that innocence is kept within as without. Anger properly is a commotion of passion. Anger which is from a cause and not from passion is judgment, not an unlawful commotion.

He does not say, “whoever desires,” but “whoever looks at her to lust after her”, that is, who attends with this end and intention, that he should desire her, which is no longer a mere titillation, but full consent to lust, so that, if the opportunity exists, it is carried out. 55_marg551: Bede. A great addition. Sight is put for every movement which is toward delight, not only bodily but interior, which is in concupiscence, in which those eyes are opened which, as punishment for sin, are read to have been opened badly to the first parents; then one proceeds to the affection of the heart, and the will is not lacking, only the occasion of sin. Just as, therefore, a good will is rewarded when the power to act is lacking, so deliberation together with the effort of vices is condemned, because a man is accused or defended not according to what he could and was not allowed to do, but according to what he willed and purposed from conscience.

55_marg554: The eye may be taken as a beloved friend, a counsellor, as one who shows the way; the right eye, the one who is in divine things. But he who gives counsel in matters pertaining to the body is likewise an eye. He scandalizes, that is, if he wishes to draw one into some heresy. Likewise the right hand is called a ‘friend’, who is a friend in divine things. The left, one who is in the necessities of this life. As sight suits the eye, so action suits the hand. Or in the eye and in the right hand may be understood brothers, a wife, sons, relatives, if there are any who are an impediment, whom we ought to separate from ourselves, lest while we wish to gain them, we ourselves perish. Whence in Leviticus it is said of the high priest: ‘Whose soul is given over to the worship of God, lest he be defiled over father and mother or daughters’, that is, he should know the affection of no one except him to whose worship he is dedicated.

55_marg562: The name Gehenna is not found in the old books, but is first put by the Lord. The occasion of this name is this: there was an idol Baal beside Jerusalem, at the foot of Mount Moria, where Siloe was; this valley was watered and wooded and full of delights, and a grove in it was consecrated to idols; and the people of Israel went so mad that, leaving the temple, they sacrificed there and burned their sons to demons. And that place was called Gehennon, that is, the valley of Ennon. God threatens moreover that he will fill that place with corpses, so that it is called ‘polyandrum’, that is, a tomb of the dead. Hence, by the name of that place, the future punishments are designated.
55_interl494: likewise. A more abundant justice: there it is lawful to put away; here not except for the cause of fornication
55_interl495: it was a permission, not a precept
55_marg563: Moses wrote in Deuteronomy that if a wife does not please her husband because of some uncleanness, he should put her away. Christ explains that this was said because of the hardness of husbands, not so that separation be allowed, but so that murder be prevented. For it is better to be divided than for blood to be shed through hatred. Christ, however, excepted only fornication; he commands the other troubles to be endured for the faith of marriage and for chastity. It is not putting her away, with carnal union despised, to live with the wife spiritually. Here he commands that the wife not be put away, he who elsewhere says: “He that doth not hate his father and mother and children, etc., cannot be my disciple.” Therefore it was said: since in the kingdom of God there is no condition of the present life; whoever does not hate it, and has not wished it to end, does not yet love the kingdom of God. He therefore hates not the men, whom he rather wishes to remain with him, but the corruptible union in a wife, the wretched law of being born and dying in parents. But he loves their eternal being with himself and with all those. Just as he loves an enemy not because he is an enemy and evil, but because he is a man, that he may be saved and be with him.
55_marg564: Moses permitted a bill of divorce to be given, lest blood be shed on account of hatred. He permitted evils to be done, lest worse things be done; and in permitting this he did not show the justice of God, but took from sin the guilt of sinning, so that to those acting, as it were, according to the law, the sin does not appear to be sin. For if divorce is permitted, the evil is nevertheless lawful. For this reason the apostles commanded second marriages on account of the incontinence of men. He permitted, he did not command. What we permit unwillingly we command, because we cannot fully prohibit the evil wills of men.

55_marg567: If it happen that you swear, swear by the Creator, not by the creature. For by that by which anyone swears, he reveres it, loves it, and fears it. Therefore the law commands that one swear only by God.
55_marg568: For the Jews, swearing by angels and Jerusalem and the elements, venerated creatures with the honour of God. Therefore, just as they used to sacrifice victims to God lest they sacrifice them to idols, so it has been allowed to the weak to swear by God; not that this is done rightly, but because it is better that this be offered to God than to creatures. But Christ forbids swearing altogether, that is, lest anyone, as if it were good, seek an oath, and by constant swearing slip into perjury. For Paul also swears when he makes God witness, not because it is good to swear, but because it is necessary, since unless one swears men are slow to believe what is useful to them.
55_marg569: He who does not swear cannot forswear, as he who does not speak cannot lie.
55_interl500: I keep far from perjury while I forbid swearing
55_marg570: He teaches that nothing in creatures is so cheap that one ought to swear falsely by it, since he forbids swearing from the highest to the lowest, that is, from heaven to a hair. A man is convicted of perjury against God, whose throne is heaven and to whom whatever is belongs. It is said, ‘In heaven’, that God ‘sits and treads the earth’, not that he has members so placed, but because in the body of the world the heaven is the greatest part, the earth the least. He is said to ‘sit’, as though the more excellent beauty, being present to the lesser, judges and orders the least in the lowest things. For the seat of God signifies judgment. Mystically: heaven is the soul of the just, earth of the sinner. And because “the spiritual man judgeth all things, and he himself is judged of no man,” he is said to sit. The sinner, because he is ordered by justice in lower things and placed under the law, is called ‘the footstool of his feet’.

55_marg571: They either supposed heaven to be something more, or swearing by it they did not think themselves bound by the oath; therefore he so tempers the sentence that heaven is believed to be a creature of God and nothing more, and because it is his throne, perjury is to be feared. So too with earth, because it is his footstool. Therefore he who swears by a creature owes the oath to him who created and rules it, nor is it rightly thought to be paid to another.
55_marg572: Let us not swear by creatures so that we revere them beyond what we ought. Let us not swear by them so that we think them worthless, namely, so that when we swear by them we reckon our oaths as nothing.

55_marg606: Pray for them that persecute, etc. He does not say this for brothers, in whom sins are sometimes graver than the persecution of enemies. Whence, when John had said: “He that knoweth his brother to sin a sin which is not to death, let him ask, and life shall be given to him, who sinneth not to death,” he adds: “There is a sin unto death: for that I say not that any man ask”; where it is clearly shown that there are certain brothers for whom we are not commanded to pray. A sin unto death is when, after the knowledge of God through the grace of Christ, someone attacks the brotherhood, and against that very grace by which he has been reconciled to God is driven by the disdain of envy; which perhaps is the sin against the Holy Ghost. “A sin not unto death” is when someone has not withdrawn love from a brother, but through some infirmity of mind has not rendered the duties owed to brotherhood; whence Christ said: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” For those who were not yet sharers in the grace of the Holy Ghost had not yet entered into the fellowship of brotherhood. This difference separates Peter denying from Judas: not because the sinner is not to be forgiven, but because the stain of that sin is so great that he cannot undergo the humility of entreating, even if, by an evil conscience, he is compelled to acknowledge and enumerate his sin; as Judas, when he said “I have sinned”, despairing more easily ran to the noose than sought pardon in humility. Because of the greatness of the sin, such men are to be believed already to have the condemnation of sin; and God does not pardon this repentance, since, although they confess they have sinned, and it vehemently grieves them to have done evil, yet they have such affections of mind that they do not humble themselves to ask pardon. But it may move [one] that John in the epistle seems to admonish only that we love brothers, concerning the love of God and neighbour, whereas the Lord says that one must pray also for enemies. But brothers are understood not only as those who already believe, but also those who are about to believe, for whom one must pray, so that they may be joined to us in the fraternal covenant.

55_marg644: Bede. Among his other wholesome and divine warnings with which he counsels believers, he set out a form of prayer and handed down a discipline. In this prayer is not taught what God does not know, but what he wills to grant, to be asked for with reverence. Hence he also composed the prayer in few words, so that we may have confidence that he quickly grants what he wills to be asked for briefly. Words of this kind were not needed by him who knows all things, but so that our affection, which deals with God, might learn the things it asks for, not the words it should say. Hence it is not only these words that are prayed, but also others contained under the same and no other sense, by which our heart too is kindled. 55_marg650: The distinction of these seven petitions must be seen. For, while our life is lived in time and eternal life is hoped for, the earlier ones are eternal in dignity, yet these are received first. In these seven petitions all the good things of the present life or of the future are contained, and there is in them a wonderful order, as is read in Isaias: just as the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost begin from the highest and run down to “the beginning of wisdom,” so the order of prayers extends from the highest to the end, that we may be freed from the evils of the world. But if in both we begin from the end toward perfection, there is an order of ascent. But if from the highest (because we receive this from the heavenly things) there is an order of descent. But because through these we rise from the lowest to the highest, the seven beatitudes which are sought through the same gifts gradually reach from the lowest to the highest. So in prayers we obtain the gifts; in the gifts, that we work the commandments; from the working, the beatitudes follow. In eternal life the obtaining of the first three petitions takes place, although they begin here; for ‘the sanctification of the name’ began to be carried out from his humble coming, and ‘the coming of the kingdom’ will be made manifest at the end of the world, and the perfection of ‘the will’ will be completed by the perfection of our beatitude itself and the ending of the age. And these three, once consummated, will remain for ever. The remaining four pertain to this life. For spiritual ‘bread’, though eternal, nevertheless pertains to this time insofar as it is administered daily to the soul. And perhaps for this reason it is called ‘bread’, because it is learned by labour and by reasoning. Then it will be as drink, when it is drawn without labour. And now our ‘sins’ are forgiven us, and we forgive. And now ‘temptations’ harass our life. And ‘deliverance from evil’ pertains to this life, which by the justice of God we have deserved as mortal. Hence by his grace we shall be delivered.
55_marg651: This seven-part number seems to fit that from which this whole sermon flowed. For if the fear of God is that by which they are blessed (“The poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven”), let us ask that the name of the Lord be sanctified in us, with chaste fear remaining for ever and ever. If piety is that by which they are blessed (“The meek, for they shall possess the land”), let us ask that the kingdom come, either into us, that we may become meek and not resist him, or from heaven to earth in the brightness of the coming, where we shall rejoice, as it is said: “Come, ye blessed of my Father.” If knowledge is that by which they are blessed (“They that mourn: for they shall be comforted”), let us ask that the will be done, that the flesh may agree with the spirit; for there is no grief except that these things struggle against each other, so that we are compelled to say: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” If fortitude is that by which they are blessed (“They that hunger and thirst after justice: for they shall have their fill”), let us pray that daily bread be given us, by which, strengthened, we may come to that fullness. If counsel is that by which they are blessed (“The merciful: for they shall obtain mercy”), let us forgive, and pray that we be forgiven. If understanding is that by which they are blessed (“The clean of heart: for they shall see God”), let us pray not to be led into temptation by harsh or flattering things, lest the heart be not simple, since it does not seek the good simply in all that it does. If wisdom is that by which they are blessed (“The peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God”), let us pray to be delivered from evil. For deliverance makes free men, that is, sons, so that we may say in the spirit of adoption: “Abba, Father.” “Amen” signifies that in all these petitions what is asked is undoubtedly granted by the Lord, if we do not neglect to keep the covenant of the last condition. Whence he adds: If you forgive, etc.

55_marg661: As in the angels, so in men. Or as in the just, so in sinners converted. Or as in Christ, so in the Church. Or as with the mind I serve the law of God, so also with the flesh.
55_marg662: In spirit we are heaven; in flesh we are earth. For we pray that, as in heaven, that is, in spirit, so on earth the will may be done, so that flesh and spirit may be a spiritual man, of whom it is said: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.” Nor is it only prayed that we may will good things, but that the will may be done in us, so that we may live to you, not to ourselves. These three are had more perfectly in the future, but here, for the present, we pray in part, so that afterwards they may be had more perfectly. The four that follow are the safeguards of the present life.
55_interl612: the gift is fortitude; the virtue, hunger and thirst for justice
55_marg663: The hunger for justice, that it may attain to satiety, is strengthened by the spirit of fortitude. Therefore we pray: “Give us this day our daily bread,” without which we would die of hunger.
55_marg664: Bread is the body of Christ, or the Word of God, or God himself, whom we need daily, or who is above all substances.
55_marg665: This is: “the living bread which came down from heaven,” whose sublime nature is above all substances.
55_marg666: Ours. Because Christ has been made ours, and God the Father with Christ has given us all things. Therefore we pray that what is ours by gift may be given to us daily in effect.
55_marg667: Or ‘daily’, because: “They that eat me shall yet hunger.” Here it is daily; in the homeland it is eternal. This bread ought to refresh us constantly within, through faith and charity, because without it no one can live. Or the spiritual precepts are called bread, which are always to be practised or kept.
55_interl615: that we may return free to the homeland
55_interl616: the gift is knowledge, the virtue grief
55_marg668: After food he asks for forgiveness of sins, so that he who is fed by God may live in God and come to eternal life.
55_marg669: When we say ‘forgive us our debts’, we ask for the spirit of knowledge, by which we understand sins, which without the spirit of knowledge are not understood. For knowledge indeed belongs to the use of temporal things, and it is the virtue for avoiding evils and seeking goods, so that we may weep over our own and others’ contagions and desire the good things. There are three great degrees, for he who is delivered from evil already clings to the highest good. The one delivered asks his deliverer that he not be led again into temptation. But because in this life not even the just live without sin, he asks to be freed from that, so that he may know what he ought to owe his brothers out of charity. But because we do not yet enjoy the vision of God, food is necessary on the way, so that some day we may come to the homeland. Hence we ask for bread, which no one reaches without the spirit of fortitude; where then is fortitude, there is hunger for justice. For eternal food is the fullness of justice. It is daily, because we daily fill ourselves with it, hungering for it.
55_interl620: on that condition; otherwise the whole prayer has no fruit
55_marg670: See by what caution we are bound. In it he also bends us to mercy towards one another, and promises pardon to those who sin against him, and promises pardon to us, and through us to others.
55_marg671: We must not deny pardon for a fault. Whence: “When you pray, forgive, if you have aught against any man; otherwise your Father will not forgive you your sins.”
55_marg672: It is permitted to demand money back from someone, but we never justly deny pardon of sins to one who asks.
55_interl622: the gift is piety, the virtue meekness
55_interl623: Led into temptation is he who is broken by temptation.
55_marg673: And lead us not. But enlighten us by the spirit of knowledge, that we may know by what evils we are entangled; and that our tears may avail, we pray: “Forgive us our debts.”
55_marg674: Not that he himself leads us into it, but because he forsakes us and allows us to go. Nor does he pray not to be tempted, but not even to be overcome for a little; for temptation is necessary for the crown.
55_marg675: And do not, by abandoning us in temptation, let us be overcome, even if you let us be tempted; without which no one is proved.
55_marg676: From evil: from every evil, visible and invisible. This deliverance is daily necessary, since we do not live without evil of soul and body. But it will be completed at the end, when we shall be immortal and impassible.
55_marg677: This one petition contains as much as all the preceding ones.
55_marg678: So that, by the spirit of the fear of God, all harmful things within and without may be driven out, and we may live blessedly in poverty.
55_marg679: Do not let us be led into that which is not yet, and deliver us from that in which we are led. Having done this, there is nothing to fear, nothing left to pray for.
55_marg680: From the lowest to the highest one thus ascends by degrees. We are delivered from evil through the spirit of fear. Thence delivered, we desire to be poor in spirit and in things, when we say: “And lead us not into temptation.” We ask for the spirit of piety, that the inner man may be tamed and become meek, so that he may not be moved by temptation.
55_marg681: We must labour by prayers that we may receive the gifts from grace. We must act by the gifts, that we may come to merits; for merits, blessedness is to be hoped. Otherwise one arrives neither at the gift without prayers of faith, nor at blessedness without merits.
55_marg682: Nothing is lacking that is not contained in these seven petitions, whether it pertains to the present life or to the future life.
55_marg683: Christ has handed down very concisely not only the discipline of the commandments but also that of prayers and gifts, so that in few words he might commend many necessary things to memory, and so that the simplicity of faith might quickly learn the sufficiency of its salvation, and the prudence of the clever might be more amazed at the depth of the mysteries. Hence Isaias: “a short word shall the Lord make upon the earth.” For since he shortened it so that it might be grasped by memory, so he filled it with things that no one can perceive without the grace of the Holy Ghost.
55_marg684: He has laid down the form by which we wish to be judged. Whence, to those who forgive, confidence before God answers with obtaining; but to the exacting, the punishment of vengeance or damnation bites.
55_marg685: God prefers to find someone to whom he may show mercy rather than someone whom he may punish. Therefore he has placed in our power with what conscience each one provokes God’s judgment toward himself, and how he may temper the sentence of so great a danger. We all owe, and the Father’s indulgence is necessary for all. Therefore let us forgive others from the heart, so that greater or more things may be remitted to us.
55_marg686: This is concluded at the end, so that it may be certain to us what we have promised in our prayers; nor does the judge whom we ask require anything else than that we be to our brethren such as we ask him to be to us. And he who does not do this is guilty twofold: first, because he has sinned and is in debt; then, because, admonished by the judge, he does not forgive his brother. Whence: “And when you shall stand to pray, forgive, if you have aught against any man; otherwise your Father will not forgive you.”
55_interl628: the men against whom they sin
55_marg687: But if you will not forgive men, etc. No excuse is left, because each one will be judged in the future according to this sentence. From this it is clear that each one is condemned in his own unbelief.
55_interl630: “Judgment without mercy shall be to them that have not done mercy.”
55_marg688: After he taught how we ought to pray, he teaches about fasting, which again pertains to purity of heart, lest it be not simple toward God while it is drawn to outward things.
55_interl631: that is, to show off the fast by the very sadness of the face
55_marg689: He does not forbid the virtue, but the feigned appearance of virtue.
55_marg690: It is good to be sad for one’s sins with fasting, for repentance, and to humble our soul. Whence: “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise.” But he forbids the sadness that is sought for praise. Therefore he does not say simply: ‘Do not fast’, but adds: as the hypocrites, sad.
55_interl632: actors playing another’s part, who strive not for virtues but stir up the favour of the crowd
55_interl633: ‘demoliuntur’ for ‘exterminant’; this is properly said of exiles
55_marg691: That is, they draw them outside the limits of the human condition. As boasting is in the brightness of clothes, so it is in excessive squalor and leanness.
55_marg692: To demolish is as it were to scatter, and to reduce the beauty of the face as it were to nothing.
55_marg693: With mournful squalor, in which there is also boasting; and they deceive all the more under the appearance of religion.
55_marg694: Note that sheep ought not put off their skins, but be clothed, if at any time wolves cover themselves with them.
55_interl634: here he rebukes the end of the intention, as above
55_interl635: that they may seem unlike others, and by that very squalor be extolled above other men
55_interl636: the praise they wanted, not the adoption of sons
55_interl637: he speaks to one as to all
55_interl638: he anoints the head who is made fat inwardly with spiritual joy
55_marg695: Refresh the mind with spiritual joy on the days of abstinence, so that the odour of love may blaze in works of mercy. Wash the conscience with tears, so that it may be clean before God. For a work of mercy does not suffice without a clean conscience, nor this without that.
55_marg696: It was the custom among the Palestinians to anoint the head at feasts; therefore anoint your head, that is, show yourself festive and cheerful, and refresh your mind with spiritual oil, and do not seek outward praise for the fast. But since you turn away from the world, rejoice before God; and so you will cleanse your face, that is your heart, from squalor; these being removed, it will be permitted to see God.
55_marg697: Behold, not everything in the New Testament is to be taken literally. For they would be ridiculous, anointed with oil, in a fast; but the mind ought to be anointed with the spirit of love of him in whose sufferings we ought to share by mortifying ourselves, and not with the oil of flattery; otherwise fasts are empty.
55_marg698: Christ has been made ointment for us, which, poured out through the passion of death, filled his Church with its fragrance. Therefore we ought to fast for no other cause, but, drenched with his Spirit, by abstinence mortifying the flesh, we share in his passion. Let us then be anointed by him, so that works of mercy may be heaped up and love poured out within; for without him the cup of our fast is not inebriated with the affection of piety.
55_marg699: He fasts for God who mortifies himself for love of him, and what he takes from himself he bestows on another.
55_interl640: he fasts for men who courts their favour
55_interl643: another explanation: through faith in the heart
55_interl644: in conscience, where he himself is
55_marg700: And your Father. The Father is within through faith, and repays deeds done in secret. Therefore one must fast there where he may see. And the one who fasts must so fast that he pleases him whom he carries in his breast.
55_interl645: it depends on what was said: That you appear not to men fasting
55_interl646: storing up riches, that is, placing hope in earthly things
55_marg701: Lay not up, etc. He commands that earthly things be given out for purity of heart.
55_marg702: He who fasts, either by keeping what he does not eat, or by seeking glory, lays up treasure on earth. He who does so for God’s sake lays up in heaven, that is in eternity; although the warning is specially about almsgiving, it is nevertheless taken of every work of virtue, because whatever is done for God we shall receive eternally in him. Rust consumes metals, the moth garments, and thieves take what is untouched by these. In these three ways every avarice is condemned, for all things that are possessed pass away. Morally. If we do something in the flesh, we store up treasures on earth when we occupy the precious senses of the body with earthly desires, which rust, that is lust, consumes. Moreover, anger and pride and the other vices destroy the garments of character; and whatever of these remains, the demons steal.
55_marg703: Everything earthly is consumed either by rust, as gold and silver, or dissolved by rot and worms, like a garment; or what is immune from these is taken by thieves, like precious stones. In these, therefore, every kind of avarice is rebuked.
55_marg704: Allegorically. Rust signifies pride, which dims the beauty of the virtues. The moth, which secretly gnaws garments, is envy, which also tears good zeal and scatters the bond of unity. The thieves are heretics and demons, who are always intent on this: to despoil spiritual things.
55_interl651: that is, heretics and demons, who are always intent on this, to despoil spiritual things
55_interl652: not for me, to whom it does not profit, but for you
55_marg705: As if he said: when you fast, or do some good work, store it there where corruption cannot approach.
55_marg706: That is, place all hope in heavenly things, walking by faith, embracing charity.
55_marg707: That is, in the spiritual firmament, which does not pass: “Heaven and earth shall pass, but my words shall not pass.” If then the heart is in heaven, it is clean, because heavenly things are clean. But if it wallows on earth, how is it clean? That is, if it does something to attain earthly things, how is it clean? For though those things are clean in their own kind, a more worthy thing is soiled as it is mixed with an inferior, as gold with silver, silver with lead.
55_interl654: because the future riches of the saints are incorruptible
55_interl656: because there no deceit of the devil will prevail against the elect of God
55_marg708: If on earth, the heart is downward; if in heavenly things, the heart is fixed in Christ.
55_interl657: universally: of money and of all the pleasures of this age; of this kind of treasure is gluttony, of this kind lust, and the like
55_interl658: by whose intention, deservedly, works are discerned whether they are of light or of darkness
55_marg709: He pursues purity of heart. As the eye directs the limbs to work, so intention and the light of faith direct all virtues. The lamp is light in a vessel; so charity is in faith. When faith shall cease, charity alone will shine.
55_marg710: From the outer he teaches the office of the inner man: by the intention of the mind and the light of faith all the virtues are illumined, so that they make the body bright.
55_marg711: Likewise, this passage is in itself about purity of heart, or about the grace of the earlier works that appear openly.
55_interl659: one and pure, of which in the Canticles: “Thou hast wounded my heart with one of thy eyes,” that is, in charity
55_marg712: If with pure intention you do the good you can, your works are works of light, even if they do not seem so to men. If the intention is perverse, whatever is done is wicked, even if it seems right. The eye is one and simple: namely charity, which now shines in faith as in a vessel.
55_interl660: that is, the whole collection of virtues, or the whole action
55_marg713: If the intention is not from faith, the whole inner man is dark, because whatever is not from faith is sin.
55_marg714: Since intention, following after, shapes the work. Therefore if the good things you do become darknesses because they are done with an evil intention, what of those things which are evil in themselves and are done with an evil intention?
55_marg715: The intention with which we do whatever we do, which is known in us, is called ‘light’. But the outcome of the thing is uncertain: when I give or do something for someone, I do not know whether it turns out for good or for ill to him; and therefore he calls it ‘darkness’. He says, therefore: if the intention with which you act, which is known to you, is soiled by the desire of temporal things, how much more the deed itself, whose outcome is doubtful; because even if it turns out well for another, what you do without good intention will profit you nothing. For how you did it is imputed to you, not how it befell him.
55_interl662: evil things that are done with perverse intention
55_interl663: as if: I cannot store up treasure and serve God
55_marg716: As if you could not do good in the sight of men and at the same time please God, nor store up treasure alike in heaven and on earth, nor serve both vices and virtues. Whatever you do, you do either from love of God or from the slavery of the devil.
55_marg717: Since the kingdom of God and that of the devil are at odds with each other, no one can serve in both at once. Whence those who are baptized renounce the devil and his works.
55_interl664: that is, to store up treasure in heaven and on earth
55_interl666: to those at odds with each other
55_marg718: There is no middle. For whatever you do is either from love of God or from the slavery of the devil.
55_marg719: Indeed the devil is to be hated, and God to be loved. For no one has ever openly hated God; all confess that they love him, and they curse the name of ‘devil’; although the vicious endure him as a tyrant dominating over them, they do not hold God in hatred but despise him, overcome by their own lust and the persuasion of the devil.
55_marg720: Augustine. He does not indeed love him, for no one loves the devil. But entangled in his own lust he endures him, as one who, joined to another’s maidservant, because of his own lust endures harsh servitude, although he does not love the one whose maidservant he loves.
55_interl670: he sets God second, though he loves his commandments
55_marg721: He will not indeed hate him, for no one’s conscience can hate God. The same, in the Retractations, on the same matter: “I do not see that it should have been said. For there are many of whom it is written: ‘The pride of them that hate thee ascendeth continually,’” etc.
55_interl671: he expresses who the two masters are
55_interl672: a good steward is not a slave
55_interl673: that is, riches: it is indeed lawful to have them, but not to serve them
55_marg722: Mammon, in the Syrian tongue, is riches, which to serve is to deny God. He does not say to have, which it is lawful to do, that one may dispense well, but to serve, which is of the covetous. This name is said to belong to the demon who presides over riches, not because they are in his power, but because he uses them to deceive, ensnaring with the snares of riches.
55_interl674: do not be drawn back from eternal things by care for these, because they are nothing
55_marg723: Therefore, because you cannot serve God and Mammon. Be not solicitous, which is to serve riches. Throughout the whole sermon he has commanded contempt of the world and trust in the future, while he bade us endure evils, not avenge them, love enemies, and flee human glory. Now he wishes to confirm this by faith in the hope of eternal things, because there are many whom love of present things and despair of future things make sluggish.
55_marg724: Bread is got in the sweat of the face; but labour is to be exercised, and care is to be taken away, which disturbs the mind while it fears that either possessions will perish or what has been toiled for will not be attained.
55_marg725: “Of your soul,” that is, to the animal nature, to which these things are necessary. Commit all your hope to God, because you can acquire or keep nothing except what he has decreed.
55_marg726: Here soul is put for life, which is sustained by food, as there: “He that loveth his life shall lose it.”
55_marg727: The animal life is sustained by food in another way, and this is put for life; it lives with the beasts; but he who loses it for Christ will find it spiritual, unto eternal life.
55_interl675: because this is to serve riches
55_marg728: Life is not for the sake of food, nor the body for the sake of clothing, but for the Church. Therefore let not the mind be anxious, so that it may receive what was created for its own sake.
55_marg729: As he who gave greater things, that is life and body, will also give lesser things, that is food and clothing. Let no one doubt these promises of truth. Let man be what he ought to be, and straightway all things are added to him for whose sake they were made.
55_marg730: This is about food. The saints are rightly compared to birds, because they seek heaven; and some are so removed from the world that now they do nothing on earth, but already live in heaven by contemplation alone, of whom it is said: “Who are these that fly as clouds?” etc.
55_marg731: These examples do not forbid foresight, nor labour, but anxiety, so that all your trust may be in God, since even birds live without care.
55_interl678: they are fed without care by God’s providence
55_interl679: then much more you who are sons
55_marg732: He magnifies and confirms the trust of sons, because if the goodness of the Father extends even to those things, how much more to the sons of adoption?
55_interl680: then much more you who are rational, to whom eternity is promised
55_interl681: because rational and adopted into sons
55_interl682: by his own care and cleverness
55_marg733: And which of you, by taking thought, can add to his stature by one cubit, etc. Leave, then, the care of governing the body to him who brought it to this measure.
55_marg734: Not that labouring and providing for this is unbecoming, but all anxiety is to be cast aside, and hope is to be placed in God.
55_interl683: Above about food, here about clothing.
55_marg735: He confirms the exhortation about clothing with a fitting example.
55_interl685: These are not allegorical, but so that greater things may be persuaded from lesser ones.
55_interl687: so that they make clothing for themselves
55_marg736: What purple of kings, what embroidery of weavers, can be compared with flowers? The colour itself is called ‘the covering of flowers,’ as we say: ‘a blush has covered that man.’
55_marg737: If those things which serve only for the time and quickly fall away are to be burned in the fire, God adorns them so beautifully.
55_marg738: Tomorrow is put for the future in the Scriptures, as Jacob says: “My justice shall answer for me tomorrow.”
55_marg739: Into the oven. Other books have: ‘Into the fire’ or ‘Into the heap,’ which has the appearance of an oven.
55_marg740: How much more, namely, he will clothe. And therefore all trust is to be placed in him. But if we are not confident about these things, how do we hope for invisible things? That faith is very slight which is not sure even about the smallest things. Therefore he also instils trust about eternal things, and condemns unbelief.
55_interl693: you who are in the image of God and called to eternal things
55_marg741: Whoever doubts in any promise is of little faith. And the more he doubts, the less he finds those things for which he was anxious.
55_interl694: He does not say, ‘Do not seek.’
55_marg742: He inculcates and repeats more fully what he taught from the start of the discourse, so that we may live without anxiety.
55_marg743: Here seem to be rebuked those who, scorning common food or clothing, seek for themselves finer or plainer food or clothing than those with whom they live.
55_interl695: that is, do not let yourselves be hindered by the care of such things from toiling for heavenly things
55_marg744: Anxiety chokes the word of God so that it does not bear fruit, and makes a man like a Gentile, that is, an unbeliever.
55_marg745: What, then, does he have more than a Gentile, whose unbelief troubles his mind and wears him down with the cares of this life?
55_marg746: Those for whom there is no care about the future. But it is for sons to seek the kingdom.
55_interl696: while you hear ‘Father,’ do not doubt about his will
55_interl697: who does not shut his heart to good sons
55_marg747: These things are provided by God, who knows that these things are necessary for us on our way.
55_marg748: Thus he makes sons secure, through the goodness and providence of the Father, free from worldly care.
55_interl698: and he gives them, unless your unbelief turns him away
55_interl699: let this be your chief intention
55_marg749: Here he plainly shows that these things are not to be sought as our goods, although they are necessary. The kingdom of God, however, is to be sought, and in it our end is to be placed, for the sake of which we do all things; for example: we eat in order to preach the gospel, we do not preach in order to eat. When he says ‘first,’ he signifies that this other is later, not in time but in dignity. For that is to be sought; this is necessary for the sake of that. Therefore, ‘seek first the kingdom of God,’ that is, put it before all other things. But that you may seek this, anxiety ought not to underlie your seeking, lest those things be lacking. For your Father knows, as he said, that you have need of these things; and therefore he did not add, ‘Then seek these things,’ but said, ‘These shall be added,’ that is, consequently and without any hindrance, if you seek those things. Nor does he say, ‘Those things will be given,’ but ‘added,’ because one thing is given principally, another is added over and above; because in intention there ought to be eternity, in use temporality; and the one is given, the other added.
55_interl701: do all things for the sake of that
55_interl702: not that it comes after these things, but because it is the highest, sought for its own sake, beyond which nothing is sought
55_interl703: which he also gives, unless your unbelief averts it
55_marg750: Let us seek the kingdom of God by pursuing his justice. The justice of the kingdom, however, is to observe all that Christ taught. To seek the kingdom is to fulfil justice itself by works, solely so that God may be glorified and that we may please him in all things.
55_marg751: The kingdom of God is the supreme good, and therefore is to be sought. It is sought by faith, hope and charity.
55_interl704: that through him, and not through yourselves, you may be just; by justice one comes to the kingdom
55_interl705: the justice of the kingdom is what he taught above: ‘unless your justice abound’
55_interl706: to be used on the way, for the sake of that and not for their own sake
55_marg752: Because all things belong to sons, and therefore all these things will be added, even to those not seeking them; if they are taken away, it is for a trial; if they are given, it is for thanksgiving, because “all things work together unto good.”
55_interl707: because these accompany the intention of eternal things
55_interl708: because all things will be added
55_marg753: By fear, grief, and the anxiety of cares, which disturbs the mind.
55_interl709: not labour and foresight is condemned, but the anxiety that chokes the mind
55_marg754: That is, for the future; for the present he allows it. Whence the Apostle: “We worked night and day, lest we should be chargeable to any of you.” About future things, which divine ordering provides for, it is not fitting to be anxious; rather, receiving present things with thanks, let us leave the care of the future, which is uncertain, to God, to whom we are a care. He calls the care of present things ‘malice,’ because it is penal; for it pertains to this mortality, which we have deserved by sinning, which is burdensome enough in itself, and we ought not add the evil of our own anxiety. No one should be scandalized if he sees one of the just provide the necessities for himself and his own, nor judge him to be thinking about tomorrow, because he who commanded this, to whom angels ministered, had a money-bag for the sake of giving this example, so that he might supply necessities for use; Judas was the keeper of it. Hence it follows: Judge not, etc.
55_marg755: Not the day which the Lord made, but the one which Job and Jeremias cursed, namely the one the devil found.
55_interl711: for then you will care about that day itself, and not about what is before it
55_marg756: And because the mind is overwhelmed by present care, the evil of the day ought not be doubled.
55_interl713: the day is not evil, but evils happen in it
55_interl714: not sin, but the labour and distress of the world
55_marg757: About doubtful matters, since judgment is made about manifest things, and not about those things about which it is uncertain with what intention they are done; about these no one judges without danger.
55_marg758: It is rash judgment when those to whom judgment has not been committed judge, whether about manifest or hidden things. Judgment, however, is committed either to the teachers of the Church or to the princes of the earth. If these, then, judge about manifest things, namely those that are convicted or confessed, they do not judge rashly. But if they judge about uncertain things, they judge rashly; this is what he forbids.
55_marg759: There are two matters in which rash judgment is to be avoided. For there are certain middle and uncertain things, done with an uncertain intention, which can be done both well and badly. For we do not know what sort he will be who now appears evil; to despair of his correction and to rebuke him when he is cast down is rash judgment.
55_interl717: that is, the judgment itself is the cause why you are judged by God
55_marg760: As if he said: ‘In whatever will you did good, in that you will be freed, and in whatever you did evil, in the same you will be punished.’ For these things are about those things in which we offend either by judging rashly, or are excused while acting rightly; and therefore he adds, ‘in what measure.’ And justly, those whose will had no end of sinning, although their sins had an end, have no end of vengeance; and those for whom judgment was without mercy shall be judged without mercy.
55_marg761: Not that God judges us rashly and repays with an unjust measure. But it is as if he said: the very rashness of judging, and the unjust measure, harms you and punishes you; and it is often not he of whom you speak who is such. ‘He who strikes with the sword will perish by the sword’: that is, by the sin of this matter he will perish.
55_interl719: that is, you will be punished with the penalties of your evil judgment
55_interl720: the measure of the punishment will be according to the measure of the fault, even if it is eternal
55_marg762: This measure can be understood as follows: in it one thing is measured, such as wheat, and another is measured, such as barley; and there is a different quantity, as one bushel from one (grain) and a hundred from another. God does so, and not unjustly, to those (who sin) in eternity.
55_marg763: And the very infamy or evil you have inflicted is the cause why you incur the due punishment.
55_marg764: Justly, those who want to enjoy sin eternally find eternal punishment; and those whose will had no end of sinning will have no end of torment.

As when, full of hatred or envy or malice, they condemn in him what he does wrong: anger, which is like a mote; hatred, like a beam. One who is angry with someone sometimes wants him corrected; one who hates cannot will this, and so it is said to be impossible for him to remove a mote from his brother’s eye who carries a beam. For first the beam of hatred, envy, pretence and all malice must be cast out, so that thus, mercifully, with respect to God and not to ourselves, we may rebuke our brother; so that whether the correction profits him or not, we may yet be secure in the simplicity of our eye.

From the start of the discourse he taught the sons of the kingdom justice, and removed their minds from anxiety. To seek the kingdom first, however, is to love God before all things and above all things, and then to carry out the work of love.
55_marg782: ASK. As if one conscious of his weakness said: what holy thing do you bid me hide, or what pearls do you forbid me to give, which I do not feel I have? Against these things he adds: ‘Ask’: as one weak in the feet first asks that he may be healed, then seeks that he may find the way which leads to his purpose, then, when he has come there, knocks that it may be opened. Thus the asking is first for health, that strength may be given to the mind by which it can fulfil what he commands. Once strength has been received, the second is the search for the way; for what are strengths to those going astray? When the way has led to the destination, the third is the knocking, that what is closed may be opened; and this fits well. For since the blessed life is completed by action and knowledge, action longs for the faculty of strength, knowledge for the manifestation of things. Of these, the first is asked, the second is sought: the former that it may be given, the latter that it may be found. But in this second, knowledge of the way comes before possession. And whoever has found the true way will come to possession, which will be opened only to one who knocks.

The others put Matthew first, and prudently keep silent about the publican. He himself puts himself second and says ‘publican,’ so that “where sin abounded, grace did more abound.” Thomas, ‘abyss’ or ‘twin,’ in Greek ‘Didymus,’ because the longer he doubted than the others, the more deeply he recognised the truth of the resurrection. Matthew, ‘given.’ James the son of Alphaeus, who is also the brother of the Lord, because he was the son of his aunt Mary, who is called Mary of Cleophas; or because Alphaeus was also called ‘Cleophas,’ or because, he having died, she married Cleophas after James was born. Thaddeus, ‘little heart,’ that is, ‘cultivator of the heart.’ By another name he is called Judas, brother of James, brother of the Lord, as he says in his epistle. Simon, to distinguish him, ‘Cananean,’ from Cana, a village, which is interpreted zeal; whence also ‘Zelotes,’ that is, emulator. Judas Iscariot, from a village where he was born or from the tribe of Issachar, received a name that foreshadowed his damnation, because Issachar, which is said to mean ‘reward of perdition,’ hints at the prize. Scariot is interpreted ‘memory of death,’ because he did not carry out the crime on a sudden persuasion but after long meditation; he was chosen among the apostles with foresight, because the truth is so great that not even a hostile minister can weaken it; and it was willed that he be deserted and betrayed, as a test of human frailty, and he bore it with moderation. Two and two are named individually, so that the companionship of pairs may be approved. These are the twelve sons of Jacob, the twelve princes of the people of Israel, the twelve springs found at Elim, the twelve stones in the priest’s garment, the twelve loaves of proposition, the twelve spies sent by Moses, the twelve stones of the altar, the twelve stones lifted from the Jordan, the twelve oxen under the bronze sea, the twelve stars in the bride’s crown, the twelve foundations, the twelve gates of the city. 55_marg1360: Note that Christ himself makes alive inwardly, and grants to ministers the power of loosing after life has been restored. For they cannot loose anyone unless the one they loose is alive. But why do they receive the power of loosing, when the one they loose has already been freed and made alive by God? Some say that the ministers loose, that is, they show the loosed to be reconciled to the Church, those whom they had earlier shut out from entering the Church because of a crime made manifest or proved. Others say that a man is purged of a certain inability to do good, which remains after forgiveness and satisfaction, and which is the dregs and remnant of previous sins, though not sin itself, when he is reconciled to the Church through the judgment of the priest. For just as after a fever some weakness remains in a man, which is not the fever itself, and from which he is not quickly purged; so in a man after the forgiveness of a crime, for which he underwent the judgment of the Church, a weakness of that sin itself remains. Others, adhering to the truth and the gospel, say that the ministers of the Church loose from sin. For the truth says: “Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them.” On this again, Augustine against the five heresies. Nor let us listen to those who deny that the Catholic Church can forgive all sins. For they do not understand the rock in Peter, and not understanding that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to the Church, they have lost them from their own hand. Against them is set the fact that God alone raised Lazarus, and handed him over to the apostles to be loosed; likewise, that to forgive sin belongs to God alone. To this they say that God first raised Lazarus, that is, that he forgives sin of himself and not from another. Since the disciples loose the one who was raised, they have it from God and not from themselves that they forgive sins. Thus it is said: “God alone forgives sin,” because what we do through him, he himself does.

55_marg1426: WHOSOEVER SHALL SCANDALIZE, etc. And if this is said generally against all, yet here it is said specifically against the apostles, who here seem to contend about dignity, and in this they could destroy others. The asses’ millstone is so called according to the custom of the province, where this penalty is for greater crimes. It is expedient for him, for it is much more useful for the innocent to end life by the most grievous penalty than, by harming a brother, to earn eternal death. Or by the asses’ millstone is expressed the round and toil of secular life; by the depth of the sea, final damnation. Whoever therefore, having the appearance of holiness, destroys the others by word or example, it would be better for him that earthly acts bind him under his outward habit to death, than that he should show holy offices to others as imitable in fault; for if he alone fell, the penalty would torment him more tolerably. Otherwise: the ass at the millstone is the pagan blind man at the stone he adores; when he has inflicted persecution on a Christian, he is punished by this penalty, that with the millstone of his own sacrilege he be drowned in the waves of the judging world. Note that as far as you can without sin, you ought to avoid your neighbour’s scandal. But if it is of the truth, the truth ought not to be abandoned for the sake of scandal.

55_marg1441: GREGORY. Because “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” the angelic nature persisting in highest blessedness. Others think that the ninety-nine is understood as the number of the just, and the one as that of sinners. Whence elsewhere: “I am not come to call the just, but sinners.” In Luke it is written: “There is greater joy upon one sinner that doth penance, than upon ninety-nine just who need not penance.” Because, as we daily experience, those who have committed no unlawful things often indulge themselves in lawful things, and do not anxiously pant after heavenly things; and because they are secure, they remain slow to do good. On the contrary, the sinner for the most part does otherwise. There is therefore greater joy over him than over a just man who stands, as a commander does in battle; for he loves more that soldier who, returned after flight, bravely presses the enemy, than the one who never fled nor ever acted bravely. But there are also some just men over whom there is such joy that no penitent can be set before them; who, though they are not conscious of evils, so far reject even lawful things, and humble themselves in all things. How great, then, is the joy if the just man humbly laments, since it is so great if the unjust man condemns what he has done wrongly?

55_marg1516: The denarius bears the image of the king, and once was counted as ten coins. The more one labours in the cultivation of the Church by persisting in the commandments of the decalogue, the more one is formed into the image of the King, who is God. Preachers are workers, and so is each one while he persists in good work in right faith. At the morning, the third, sixth and ninth hours: the ancient and Hebrew people, who worshipped God in right faith among the elect; at the eleventh, the Gentiles are called. The differences of the hours can also be noted in each one through the moments of the ages. Morning, indeed, is the childhood of our understanding; the third hour is adolescence, because the sun is already rising high; the sixth is youth, when the fullness of strength is consolidated; the ninth is old age, when the sun, that is, the heat of life, goes down; the eleventh is a decrepit age. In all these, some are led to a good life. He who lives for himself is rebuked as idle. He who postpones even to the last age is rightly told: “Why do you stand here all the day idle?” that is, repent at least at the last.

But he who came not to call the proud just, but the humble penitents, to whom a humble confession of evils is more pleasing than a proud boasting of goods, adds: “Friend, I do thee no wrong.” They do not grieve as if defrauded of their wage, but, in the manner of the envious, that those receive more than they deserve; and they do not so much wish to receive more themselves as wish that others receive nothing or the least, as if their reward were diminished by the company of another.
55_marg1522: MURMURED AGAINST THE MASTER OF THE HOUSE, etc. It is asked how those who receive are said to have murmured, when in that blessedness all envy and murmuring must be altogether removed. But this is the custom of divine Scripture: when it treats of many in a gathering, it ascribes some things only to some of that gathering, and not to the whole gathering, according to that of the prophet: “And he brought them out with silver and gold”; and then: “And he brought them into the mountain.” Yet those who went out of Egypt, all except Caleb and Josue, died in the desert on account of their unbelief, and their sons were brought into the mountain of sanctification. So also among the first receivers, some and not all murmur, though they nonetheless receive afterwards. As it often happens that many served the Lord for long times, while others were soon, at the beginning of their conversion, carried off by martyrdom or in some other way to receive the denarius, so those who laboured long, hearing that others are at once transferred to the reward while they themselves are detained in labour for so long, seem to murmur at the delay of the reward. It can also be said of the wicked, who indeed were good at the beginning but did not bring to its end the good they began. Whence it is not those who received the denarius, but those who did not persist in goodness, who murmur, deprived of the reward: they who were good at the beginning, and who, lacking the denarius, believed they had earned it by that beginning, for which they are counted with the first receivers.

55_marg1633: DE RESURRECTIONE, etc. This indeed he replied to the question proposed about the conditions of the resurrection. And here about the resurrection, and elsewhere about the divinity, the Lord is found to have said some things before scorners; not as one who would ‘give that which is holy to dogs, and cast pearls before swine’, but because among those who tempted him there were some who listened with profit, whom it was not right to neglect on account of the uncleanness of others.

Mystically: kingdom will rise against kingdom, and the plague of those whose speech creeps like a cancer; and famine of the word of God, shaking of the earth, and separation from faith. For the last tribulation is preceded by many, and by frequent evils lasting evils are indicated. And therefore after wars and seditions the end is not immediate, because many evils must run before to announce evils without end. Some of these come from heaven, some from earth, some from the elements, some from men. “Nation shall rise”: behold the disturbance of men. “Earthquakes”: behold the regard of wrath from above. “Pestilences”: behold the unevenness of bodies. “Famines”: behold the barrenness of the earth. “Terrors from heaven and storms”, according to Luke: behold the unevenness of the air. Therefore all things destined to be consummated are troubled, so that we who have sinned in all things may be struck in all things. Whence: “The whole world shall fight for him against the unwise.”

55_marg1714: Woe to those with child, etc. Because, weighed down by a burden, they will not be able to flee. In this, Luke agrees: “Then let those who are in Judea, flee to the mountains.” The rest he seems to say differently: “and those who are in the midst thereof, depart out.” But how, since the evangelist foretold that Jerusalem would be surrounded by an army, can those who are in the midst depart, that is, when the danger will press so hard that it cannot be escaped? That is, they depart when they are not captured by desire for this age, being ready to pass over into another life. What the others said, “And he that is on the housetop, let him not come down to take any thing out of his house,” means that they should not be inclined by any affection toward the flesh. 55_marg1798: As is gathered from John’s narrative: “Jesus therefore, six days before the pasch, came to Bethania,” and there that feast took place in which the precious ointment is recalled. From there he came to Jerusalem sitting on a colt; afterwards the things that are narrated were done or enacted in Jerusalem after this coming. Therefore from the day on which Jesus came to Bethania until the day on which all these things were done and said, we understand that four days were completed, so that the day which Matthew and Mark fixed as two days before the Pasch might fall in. Mystically: after two days of the clear light of the Old and New Testament, the true Pasch is celebrated throughout the world. The Pasch, which in Hebrew is called Phase, is named not from passion but from passing over, because the destroyer, seeing the blood on the doors of Israel, passed them over, and God, giving help to them, walked from above. Mystically: because at that feast the Lamb of God was about to pass out of this world, or to lead us out by a healthful passage, as from the Egypt of this world. Pasch is properly called ‘the one day’, on which the lamb was slain at evening, that is, on the fourteenth moon of the first month. On the fifteenth moon, when they went out of Egypt, there were unleavened days for seven days. But indifferently both Pasch is used for the days of unleavened bread, and the days of unleavened bread for Pasch; Mark says: “Now the feast of the pasch, and of the Azymes was after two days.” Luke: “The feast of unleavened bread, which is called the pasch.” Mystically: with one day of the lamb immolated, seven days of unleavened bread follow, because, Christ having suffered once, through all the time of the age we must live in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

55_marg1844: The three put it so simply. Mark alone: ‘Before the cock has twice given voice.’ If Peter’s third denial began only after the first cock-crowing, the three who say ‘before the cock crows’ would seem to lie. Likewise, if the whole thing were before it, Mark would say superfluously, ‘before it crows twice.’ But because the three began before the first crowing, they looked not at when it was to be completed but at how great it was going to be, however often it was begun. Or the whole thing was completed in the mind of fearful Peter before the first crowing, although in words it began before the first and was completed before the second. For so great a fear had invaded his mind that it made him deny three times. Matthew and Mark append Peter’s denial after Jesus went out of the house where he ate the Passover; Luke and John place it before Jesus went out from there. But we easily understand that they either recapitulated, or the others anticipated; unless it moved us more that they set down such different words, and not only words but also sayings of the Lord, by which Peter, moved, preferred that presumption of dying. So they compel us the more to understand that he expressed his presumption at different places in Christ’s discourses, and that the Lord answered him three times that he would deny him before the cock-crowing, just as after the resurrection he asked him three times whether he loved him and three times commanded him to feed the sheep.

Why, then, did Matthew correct this, which he had done under the guidance of the Spirit? So that by this we might be admonished that there is such great harmony among the prophets that what is said by one is fittingly assigned to another. Or, it is found in Jeremias about a field bought, but not under this name of price; in Zacharias it is about thirty pieces of silver, and nothing about buying a field. For the evangelist interprets each of them with respect to what was fulfilled concerning the Lord, and brings into one the thirty pieces of silver, which is in Zacharias, and the field bought, which is in Jeremias. What he adds, “whom they prized,” etc., is found in neither, but must be taken from the person of the evangelist, because by a revelation of the Lord he knew that a prophecy of this kind pertained to this matter, which was done concerning the price of Christ. Indeed, in Jeremias the book of the bought field is commanded to be put into an earthen vessel; here the potter’s field is bought with the price of the Lord for a burial of strangers, that is, for the resting-place of those who are strangers with the Lord and are buried with him through baptism. In height, the contemplation of heavenly rewards. In depth, the inscrutable judgments of God. When this grace comes among men, and these things are fitted to the sacrament of the cross, then in the breadth the transverse beam is taken, on which the hands are stretched out, for the signifying of works. In the length, from that very beam down to the ground, where the whole body was, is signified to persist, that is, to remain steadfast. But in the depth, that part which lies hidden and buried in the earth, from which all that rises up springs. 55_marg1967: “In the evening of the Sabbath” etc. Mark says “very early,” in which there is no disagreement with Luke and John. Matthew, from the first part of the night, that is, from evening, signifies the night, at whose end they came to the tomb. He names it thus because from that time it was lawful to do what they wished, the Sabbath being past. “In the evening of the Sabbath,” that is, in the night of the Sabbath day. In the evening indeed they began to come, that is, to prepare spices; but they arrived as the morning dawned, which Matthew, for brevity, puts more obscurely, and others more plainly. Evening usually grows dark, but mystically he says it shines, for the glory of the resurrection. Hitherto it was said that night precedes day; now the order is changed, and the night in which he rose is joined to the day on which he showed himself. Fittingly, night used to follow day, because man had fallen from light into darkness. Now day follows night, because after the resurrection we are led from sins to life.

55_marg1991: Yet he was not seen there alone, nor was it there that he was first seen by the disciples. For Luke and John say quite plainly that on the very day of the resurrection the Lord was seen in Jerusalem first by Mary Magdalene, when it was said to her: “Do not touch me.” Then to the same woman and the other Mary as they ran to announce it to the apostles, when they also held his feet. He was seen also on the same day by two disciples on the way. He was seen also by Peter. How this came about the evangelist does not declare. He was seen also by the disciples, when they were talking in like manner, after those who knew him in the breaking of the bread had returned, and standing in the midst of them he said: “Peace be to you.” Nevertheless, Matthew and Mark write, in a spiritual sense, that the angel or the Lord himself said that he was to be seen in Galilee. Mystically indeed, because Galilee is called ‘transmigration’. For he goes before you into Galilee: that is, the grace of God, about to pass over from the Jews to the Gentiles, will go before you, preparing the way in their hearts. And there you will see him: that is, you will find his members and his living body there. Or Galilee is called ‘revelation’, not in the form of a servant, but in that in which he is equal to the Father. There he has gone before us: “When we shall be like him, we shall see him as he is.” And this is the blessed revelation, or transmigration, from this world to eternity.

55_marg2005: On the first day of the week, at dawn, as all the evangelists agree, they came to the tomb. What only Matthew tells, of the earthquake, the rolled-back stone, and the terrified guards, had already happened. Mary Magdalene came, more fervent than the others. Whence John makes mention of her, passing over in silence the others who had been with her; and seeing the stone taken away, before looking more carefully, believing the body had been taken away, she ran to tell Peter and John. They also ran to the tomb, and not finding the body they believed what Mary had said, that it had been taken away, and they went away. But Mary stood outside weeping, in the garden, namely where they had gone in. Then they saw an angel sitting upon the rolled-back stone, of whom Matthew and Mark speak. He says to them: “Fear not you; for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified,” etc. Mark did not pass over similar things. At these words, while Mary was weeping, she bent down and looked into the tomb, and saw two angels in white, sitting, one at the head, and one at the feet. They say to her: “Woman, why weepest thou? Because they have taken away my Lord; and I know not where they have laid him.” Here it is to be understood that the angels had risen, so that they were seen standing, as Luke says, who also reports them saying: “Why seek ye the living with the dead?” etc. After this Mary turned back and “saw Jesus standing, and knew not that it was Jesus,” as John says, thinking him to be the gardener; and when he named her, she recognized him, to whom it is also said: “Do not touch me.” Then she went out of the tomb, that is, out of the place hewn out in front of the stone, and with her the others, of whom Mark says: “Fear had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone.” Then, now according to Matthew: “And behold Jesus met them, saying: All hail. But they came up and took hold of his feet.” Thus we gather that they heard the address of the angels twice, as they came to the tomb, and likewise the Lord’s own address, when Mary thought him the gardener; and now he meets them again, so that the very repetition might confirm them. For Mary Magdalene came, announcing to the disciples, and the others who were with her, whom Luke mentions. There were indeed more appearances, as Paul hints when he says: “He was seen by James; he was seen by more than five hundred brethren at once”; but we read of ten in the Gospels. Five times on the very day of the resurrection. First, he appeared to Mary Magdalene weeping at the tomb. Afterwards to the same woman and the other Mary, going out to announce it to the apostles. Third, to Simon. Fourth, to Cleophas and his companion. Fifth, to them as they returned and told how they knew him in the breaking of the bread; he appeared with the doors shut, where Thomas was not present. Sixth, after eight days, when Thomas was with them. Seventh, to those fishing at the sea of Tiberias. Eighth, on the mountain of Galilee, which was not far from Jerusalem. Ninth, “while the eleven were at table,” on the day he ascended. Tenth, they saw him no longer placed on the earth, but lifted up into the air, making for the heavens, the angel saying to them: “He shall so come, as you have seen him going into heaven.”
